The house in committee of supply, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
National film board-
251. Administration.
Production and distribution of films and other visual material, $4,988,112.

I just want to say a few words about the national film board from a particular point of view. I think we in North America have a somewhat peculiar view of public agencies. We tend to regard them as likely to be havens of inefficiency, waste and mediocrity, filled with time servers. Indeed, one hears it suggested that they are the last harbour of retreat for incompetence.
In the national film board we have a government agency which derives its revenue, certainly in part, from the government, and which is responsible to parliament and therefore to the people of Canada. We know that its work could never be carried on by a commercial company, yet it is amazing to what extent this agency pays for itself. It sells its services to the extent of nearly $1,500,000, and its rentals amount to well over $500,000. Thus we must remember, when we consider the work of this agency, that parliament is not paying the whole shot.
Part of the work of the film board is to provide services for other departments of government. For example, if the Department of Agriculture or the Department of Trade and Commerce want a film made, the film board is asked to make it. I think one of the most heartening aspects about this government agency is the extent to which it has gained the confidence and won the enthusiasm of the people of Canada. One thing to be noted is that this is an example of a government agency which is not cold and impersonal, as we in North America tend to think government agencies should be. I think it is significant that this agency has gained an unique place in Canadian life, and because of this it has been able to distribute its films at only a fraction of the cost which a commercial
company would have incurred, since there are a large body of people who are willing to give their services to the board simply because they regard its work as being important to the community.
As a result of the wide distribution of the films made by the board, over 15 million people in this country have seen them either through school programs or community programs. The importance of the work of the film board to the departments of education can, in fact, hardly be rated too highly. If we include those people who have seen national film board productions by means of television, then of course the number would run into almost countless millions.
Another legend which seems to persist in North America is that the work of government agencies seldom rises above mediocrity. But, as was pointed out last night, perhaps the people of Canada do not realize the number of awards which the national film board has won by reason of the excellent quality of its work. The fact that the board has won seven of these awards throughout the world is something to be noted. It might seem that with regard to this aspect of our national life we just do not know how well our agencies are doing. We have discovered how to make films with a distinctive Canadian style. Canadian films are known because of the way they are made, and I think this shows that the flavour of Canadian life can be expressed through the medium of films. Through the films of the national film board developments in Canada have been made known in other parts of the world. This would indicate that the expenditure parliament is making on behalf of the board is worth while. I hope this will be an indication of what the role of government enterprise can be. Here is a public enterprise that is not competing with private enterprise but is giving business to and supporting private enterprise, and at the same time is making a tremendous contribution to Canadian life.
Here we have an example which shows that we can have an esprit de corps, a justifiable pride, in a public agency. Certainly the films of the board are produced with the highest degree of technical excellence. To the extent that the board changes the public image of government agencies, it is performing a remarkable service in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the minister will recall that when parliament was opened by the Queen in 1957 the national film board filmed the proceedings. I am wondering in how many places throughout Canada this film has been shown and if it is still being shown throughout the country.

Mr. Chairman, while we are locating those figures for the hon. member, perhaps I may be permitted to make a brief statement. Hon. members will notice that for the fiscal year 1961-62 the national film board estimates show an increase of $287,258. The major factor is an increase of $166,395 for salary revisions and merit increases to the board's personnel. Other increases in the operational vote are $50,000 to provide for an extension of the board's production activities, and an increase in Canadian distribution costs of $14,848 resulting from the appointment of two additional district representatives, one in British Columbia and one in Saskatchewan. The sum of $17,254 will be required for additional service and wage increases to members of the Canadian corps of commissionaires. The acquisition of equipment vote shows an increase of $18,416. The balance of $20,345 covers a number of small items.

I still have an answer coming for the hon. member for Lisgar. The reply to the hon. member is that there were 464 bookings in moving picture theatres in Canada. The picture is being shown in the schools of Canada; it is shown in every part of Canada.

I want to thank the hon. lady for giving me the answer. The reason I asked is that I have had many inquiries from the schools regarding the procedure of opening parliament. I would hope that this film would be shown extensively throughout the schools in Canada.
I might add it is available on request.
Has the national film board ever attended any international sporting event in which Canada has participated, and taken pictures of some of our Canadian athletes participating in those games?

I am told that the film board has never taken actual pictures of international competitions in which Canadian athletes participated abroad because they have never purchased the right to take those pictures, but the board does have pictures of sporting events in Canada. There is a


film which is in course of preparation-it is on the program for this year-which will deal with preparation for competition in the Olympic games.

Just by way of further comment, I know that throughout the country there is keen interest in getting copies of films of such events as the skiing championships at Squaw Valley in which Anne Heg-gtveit participated. These films, if readily available, could be shown in schools throughout the country and I am sure they would be much appreciated. My point is, can consideration be given to the national film board at least making an effort to take pictures of some of our stars at some of these future international events in order that in due course those films may be shown here and thereby encourage other amateurs to participate as well?
The film board will be very glad to consider this suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, last evening your predecessor in the chair very properly suggested, since I had included books with art, that I should defer my remarks until this particular vote was reached. I should like to say, sir, that last evening's discussion on art was most illuminating to those of us who have had little opportunity to become more than casual observers in that particular field. Some excellent addresses were made; it is not my intention to single out any one in particular, but it was a cultural evening and was well worth while.
Under this particular vote I should like to speak very briefly on the national library. One of the compensations of being a new member of parliament is the access one has to the parliamentary library, the national library, if he so wishes, and the librarians. To those of us who come from far places the contacts we make are most valuable. As an aside I should like to pay a brief tribute to the parliamentary librarian and his staff. They are always most helpful. Like the rose, I am afraid they blush unseen; nevertheless we appreciate them.
I tried to say last night that my previous knowledge of the national library was very fragmentary. I was told at one time that there were two countries in the world without national libraries, Canada and Ghana. I have learned since that Ghana now has an admirable national library and I have also

learned-one learns constantly in Ottawa- that we have the nucleus of a very promising national library in Canada.
My plea is that the promise may be fulfilled. I think it was John Ruskin who once said that books are divisible in two classes, books of the hour and books of all time. Our national library and our archives are concerned with the books of all time. We have made a start, but we need a great deal of development if the national library is to come into full fruition. My information is that there are approximately 400,000 volumes under the control of the national library. It is interesting to note that this represents one book for every 45 Canadians. To me this is pitiful when we think of the tremendous sums of money we spend in other departments which have nothing to do with the development of the Canadian mind.
The national librarian has a very difficult task. He and his staff are working in cramped quarters. They are handicapped in their endeavour to expand the facilities of their organization by not having sufficient room in which to operate. We talk and have talked in the house for the last few years about the creation of a physical green belt. We are building a glorious national capital. My plea is for the creation of a green belt of the Canadian mind, and I hope the day is not far distant when parliament will see to it that in our physical green belt there is built a national library capable of housing the tremendous store of wisdom that has come down to us through the ages and which will enrich not only our own lives but the lives of future generations. Incidentally, I note that the next generation is well represented in the galleries this morning. Generations yet unborn will profit if we establish our national library on the basis on which some of us conceive it should be established.

Mr. Chairman, I was only too happy on this occasion to defer to the hon. member for Medicine Hat who began the remarks he has made this morning on another item in the estimates, and who has made what I think is one of the most useful contributions that have been made to our debates in this session of parliament. Without any reservation whatsoever I should like to congratulate the hon. member both for what he has said and for the way in which he has said it.
It does seem to me that we are taking altogether too long to provide the building which will house the national library. It is a very fortunate thing that for the past few years, since the National Library Act was passed by parliament, we have at least been accumulating some of the books that we

I must say that I never before thought of the statistic the hon. member for Medicine Hat gave us this morning when he said that the 400,000 volumes belonging to the national library would represent one book for every 45 people in Canada. I must say I do not think that is one of the statistics I would be proud of, and I doubt if it will be put in that blue book of facts which has been published recently and which is probably not in the national library.
The plain fact is, of course, that until the national library has a real physical home it cannot expand in the way we would like to see it expand and the way it ought to expand. Until it has a proper physical home there cannot be the proper differentiation between the functions of the national library and the functions of the parliamentary library which it would be desirable to make both in the interests of efficiency and economy as between the two institutions. I do feel that it was desirable to let one of the supporters of the government have the initiative that is usually taken by the opposition on the estimates, in the hope that the observations made from this part of this side of the house might not fall on deaf ears but, coming from a supporter of the government, be received a little more sympathetically than otherwise would have been the case. I only wish that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance were not otherwise engaged at the federal-provincial conference so they could have been here to listen to what was said by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.
We do know, of course, that the site for the new national library is now occupied by No. 1 temporary building on Wellington street, which ought to have been torn down by this time. By doing so this energetic Minister of Public Works, who does a lot of talking about providing winter work, might provide a little more work this winter so the government could then proceed at once with the building of the national library. This should be done. I know the hon. lady can only use her influence with her other colleagues, that the decision will be made by the government as a whole, and particularly those members of the treasury board, on the initiative of the Minister of Public Works. At least we have the opportunity here of saying something about it, and I do hope, when the estimates of the Department of Public Works come up, the hon. member for Medicine Hat will urge the Minister of Public Works to get on with the job. From the way the hon. lady is nodding her head I think he will have her support in the cabinet, where there are secrets which she cannot reveal to us except by the expression on her face.

Possibly I might say a word about this subject. I agree with that which has been said and I thank the hon. members for their support. I too am disappointed that we have not been able to get ahead with the building before this, but possibly now that spokesmen in the house have expressed themselves I will have a little more support.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to take a somewhat different approach to that which has been taken in this debate so far. I feel that one should always be careful when speaking from a position of special knowledge, though I hardly claim as a librarian to have particularly special knowledge, but one of the points I would like to bring to the minister's attention is something I have noticed while making certain contacts with people. That is that when we have encountered historians and other people who work at the public archives, we find unstinted praise for the administration in the steps that have been taken and where expansion has taken place. Dr. Lamb, the national archivist, also happens to be the national librarian.
I cannot say I get the same reaction as I go around and encounter librarians and other people dealing with books. By this I do not mean that the criticism is nasty or vicious. I think everyone in the library profession appreciates Dr. Lamb's stature as a scholar, but there is a very definite feeling among librarians that the great ability which he brings to his role as archivist detracts from the part he might play as national librarian.
I was very appreciative, as I know were many people in the library profession, of the fact that the Prime Minister saw fit to appoint a trained librarian for the library of parliament. I have no comments to make about the person appointed, but the fact that we now have this recognition would, it seems to me, lead to the next step of the library profession in its move for recognition, and that is to have a national librarian whose training, background and interest is in libraries.
I cannot emphasize too much the favourable reaction to the work of the public archivist in the way he has expanded the types of service offered both in the library and in the manuscript sections. The microfilm facilities and that sort of thing are excellent. I think the scholarity community, especially in the fields of history and associated subjects, are very fortunate.
I would not like to suggest that the reason we have not a national library building on the way is that we have a man at the head of the public archives and national library who is in a dual function. I do not think


this is a factor, but I think librarians and people who are interested in books and the creation of a national library centre would feel somewhat happier if we had a national librarian separate from the archives.
I know this is possible. I can imagine the hon. member for Greenwood being prepared to argue that the main thing is to have a man who is a good administrator and yet has a sense of cultural values and an over all good education. I agree that this summation would apply very much to Dr. Lamb. The fact is that today there is no antithesis in library work respecting a person of a high education or intellectual status or scholarly attainments, but it is also a fact that more and more the whole organization of things in library work, as it tends towards increasing documentation, is a very specialized administrative field.
I think one of the greatest problems our society is running into lies right in this field of documentation and library work, how we are going to handle the great many records that are piling up in so many fields. I am afraid the national library is going to have a rather narrow collection, say in the field of natural science or applied science, but I am sure we can count on the national research council to provide us with a national library service in those fields. This raises the question as to what the fields the national library is going to cover and whether it is going to be primarily a documentation centre or will attempt to be the kind of large institution that has a basic collection of books in all the various fields.
I suggest that we might be 10 or 15 years behind the times if we aim to erect a huge institution built around a massive book collection. I think in Canada the emphasis should be upon keeping control of the records and books, building up a service of interchange of books, a cracker jack reference service and, through documentary control, keeping on top of all the flow of information that is pulsing into this country or in the country or about the country from anywhere in the world. That is perhaps the main challenge.
I suggest that it is into this field of specialization that librarians are moving more and more. There tends to be a picture in people's minds of a librarian as a man who reads books and book reviews and who can talk knowingly about general books that may be in a collection. As a matter of fact the best librarians-and I think we must acknowledge that the best librarians are mostly Americans -are in one sense extreme specialists in understanding techniques. I refer to punch-card techniques, I.B.M. machine techniques, the

whole business of control and making available information. The institutional kind of national library that is envisaged by many people could, I suppose, be built by a collection of one million or one and a half million volumes.
I wonder what the direction would actually be. We have a collection in Washington today of around the 15 million mark. There is a collection of between eight million and ten million books at the British museum. I have been in the Bodleian library in Oxford. At the time I was there they thought they had between five million and six million books, but they had fairly well lost control of this collection in terms of having it really available to users. The collection at Oxford that was actually available to users through catalogues and ready reference was at that time in the neighbourhood of only one million volumes. I am speaking of ten years ago.
The problem in these larger libraries is quite often, how do you get the service? I know at the Bodleian library you sometimes had to wait an hour or more for a book after you had discovered whether they had the book you wanted and where it was. The British museum is another case in point. I made inquiries there and found they had a magnificent collection and a wonderful service for scholars. They go out of their way, especially in reading room privileges, to help anyone who has a serious scholarly intent. Yet so little of their massive collection is really available. When you see the size of the collection that is available, you understand why this is so, because it is so massive.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat raised the point that we have 400,000 books within the scope of the national library. I do not know too much about the details, but I would doubt whether the national library has available in its present quarters more than 50,000 books catalogued and available. It would seem to me the main thing the national library has done, and we must give credit to the people who originated this, is that it has built up in effect a union catalogue of holdings of most of the academic libraries in Canada. This is what I mean by a type of documentation service, in other words the library acting primarily as a clearing house.
It seems to me that one of the things we are not really crystal clear about when the new building is launched is the range of the collection within the building, how big it is going to be. I think anyone in library work realizes that the initial cost of a book is really nothing in the long run if you have an institutional library. There is a changing pattern as to when the costs of storing a book match up with the costs of

In recent years, with the cost of heating and staffing institutions, this point has crept down and down until I think it is recognized by most people in university library circles that within ten years after you put a book on the shelf it has cost you as much to keep it there as it did to buy it and make the preparations to keep it. In other words the space and storage problem is a gigantic one.
If anyone thinks the flow of books is a constant thing they should go and look at some of the books available at the library. They should look at the national library Canadiana, and they will see that in the field of publishing, as in almost every other field, we have a growth potential that has been almost constant. One of the other difficulties about this growth potential and the growth rate has been the fact that publications have tended to vary so much in their format. There is all the mimeographed and other material with which hon. members are familiar. We are moving further and further away from the conventional idea of the book as a hard covered thing, and this raises great problems with regard to storage. It is easy enough to perpetuate the life of a hard covered book, but what do you do about mimeographed briefs, paperbacks, pamphlets and other things which are accumulating so rapidly today and which take so much time to catalogue?
For these reasons I think the concept of our national library needs to be reiterated in terms of the job that library is going to do, and I would suggest that the almost ceremonious conception which many people have of the national library may be already out of date in terms of the use we may possibly have for it. I know it would be very stirring to have the kind of building to which you could take a class and go into a marble hall something like the printing bureau in Hull and see illuminated manuscripts on display. Perhaps we could get Magna Carta and some of the other exhibits of that kind which are on view in the British museum in London and display them.
A service of this kind is one which reminds children of their heritage, but does it really do anything for the serious person who wants to read and study? Does it really do anything when people are able to say we have that big pile of a building filled with a collection that is worth up to a million dollars and still growing, but we are not too sure what that collection is going to be used for and what direction it is going to take. I cannot emphasize too strongly the proliferation of material and the specialization in the field

Archives, on the other hand, seem to me to be a much simpler proposition in terms of their use both by scholars and by ordinary people. They seem much closer to our history, our traditions and also to our future. The question here that interests and intrigues me, of course, is, for example, the length of time which must expire before records become free and open. For example, I am very much interested in the former member for Port Arthur. If I am ever in a position in the next decade or two to undertake the work, and if I have some available time, I would like to tackle a book or biography of this man. What about the records that he has turned over to the national archives? I quote this as an example. When are these documents to be available?
I think there is another problem which this government, particularly, has not faced; that is, giving some indication of what the members of this government plan to do with their records when their administration ends. We have never had a real definition of what is privy to a minister of the crown and what becomes, eventually, part of the public record and how long documents must form part of the public record before they are open to the scholars. I know that in Britain generally they have a 50-year rule. Sometimes this is waived, and at other times the material is held for longer than 50 years. Again, this is something in the field of public archives I should like to know something about as, I imagine, other scholars would.
There is an increasing interest which I encounter, and which I am sure other members encounter, in genealogy in this country, and here the national archives offers a service especially in connection with earlier census records. I wonder whether the archives or the national library or the national library reference centre should have this chore. I myself, again through personal interest, would like to know more of what could be done through a government agency, either the archives or the national library, toward building up an ability to trace descent not only here but in liaison with other countries. I know a problem which one of my relatives had was that of trying to trace relatives in England because of the variation in the records as between parish records before 1826 and records of births after 1826, which are usually kept in Somerset house, London. One day the Minister of Finance and I were talking and we discovered we probably had certain relationships in common two or three generations ago through families located in southern Ontario.


It seems to me that as we get older as a nation this type of tracing will attract more and more interest. I know the United States in this respect is far ahead of us in its feeling for history and looking back on family records of the past. This is an extremely important phase of reference work in the United States, and I think it is going to become much more so here. I should like to know what plans either the national archives or the national library may have to provide this particular service. I am not suggesting they are not doing a good job now, but it seems to me one can be quite positive that the demand is going to increase and that is going to mean more cost to the government. I should like to know what plans are being made for setting up a permanent service, with perhaps some definite central authority and some publications which explain how to go about the study of genealogy in Canada.
I had some specific questions I wished to ask, but in case other members may want to make some general remarks on this vote I will conclude and come back to the specific questions later.

I have a few brief comments 1 should like to make on this item. I should like to associate myself with what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has said about what we owe to the hon. member for Medicine Hat for bringing this question up. I do not think we have taken this seriously enough in the past. I have listened to the speech of the hon. member for Port Arthur, who obviously has a considerable knowledge of these things and has devoted careful thought to them. From my own experience I can say something about the dominion archivist. I know something of the extent to which he has diligently pursued historical documents and private documents which are known to be of historical interest.
My particular reason for rising is to say that I know the minister is sympathetic, and I feel that as a result of this sympathy we may be able to get this matter advanced. I understand there is no committee which is seriously considering this question now. I was greatly struck the other day on reading a book by Dr. Cyril James, president of McGill University, on a recent visit he made to Russia, and it almost frightened me to learn from his report that education in Russia is being taken much more seriously than it is here.
I asked myself some very serious questions. It was interesting to read that in Moscow, Shakespearian plays are often produced and are very well attended. Reading the other things Dr. James had to say, I was led to wonder if we are still continuing the pioneer instinct which built up this country but which

did not make us feel that libraries are one of the practical or more important things in life. I am wondering if we have reached a stage where we have to do a lot of rethinking.
We have found that part of the reason for our present unemployment situation is that we have not trained our people well enough. That to me raises the whole question of broadening education. Therefore I wanted to make my small contribution this morning in the hope that those who know more about this matter than I do may be enabled to deal with this question, which has come to have an urgency and practical importance which we have not been inclined to attribute to it in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief comments. I was most impressed by the felicitous remarks made by the hon. member for Medicine Hat, and I agree with him wholeheartedly in what he said. More surprisingly, I found myself in almost complete agreement with the hon. and learned member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate, although I thought the hon. gentleman was a bit irreverent when he spoke about a certain blue and white book because we know, of course, that historic truth should always be cherished.
I think we must urge upon the minister the pushing forward of the structural aspects, shall we say, of the national library; but, like the hon. member for Greenwood, I would rather concern myself at this juncture with the public archives in the study room of which I have spent many hours. I am tremendously impressed with the great work Dr. Lamb and his associates have been and are doing. It is extremely important that a good job be done in the national centre, because many scholars have often found that in the smaller areas throughout the provinces there is a regrettable lack of facilities of an archival nature. Therefore leadership must be given at the national level, and Dr. Lamb and his staff in my opinion are giving that leadership in a splendid way.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood on another point. I think it is sadly true that we Canadians are not an historically minded people. Probably we are not very education minded either. Perhaps this is a hangover of the frontier spirit which causes us to look upon some of these things with the eye of the Philistine.
I think of the dearth of writings concerning our great men which was mentioned by the hon. member for Port Arthur. When we leave the west end of this building we see a fine painting of Canada's fourth prime minister, Sir John Thompson, a man uniquely
qualified for leadership and who in his short career made history as an outstanding statesman, yet we find no work written about him other than what was written in a eulogistic way shortly after his tragic passing in 1894. There are, however, Thompson papers, which though not ample should, of course, be more widely and intensively used. There are two aspects to this type of situation. We must collect the papers of these great men, and we must do more about having historic research made upon them.
I believe the hon. member for Port Arthur is quite right in expressing concern about the restrictions on the records. If I had any criticism to advance with respect to the public archives of Canada I would say that they err on the side of being too restrictive with respect to the records. In that respect I feel they compare rather unfavourably with the United States in these matters. It is not every public man, of course, who like the late Mr. Arthur Meighen will leave his papers and say, "Here they are, unrevised and unrepented; so they stand for my lifetime and after". I believe that scholars should not be held too long from the papers of the men who made history. We must encourage those who are bringing about the opening up of the records of our past. I think it is up to us as national legislators to contribute in every way we can to the furtherance of this important measure.
There is one point I should like to commend to the minister. I think the study room in the archives, the one that is open 24 hours a day every day of the week, is a most splendid institution. I have often been troubled in visiting various parts of the country to discover, when I have arrived for a long week end, that I cannot have access to the records at all because everything is closed. The example set by the public archives in Ottawa is most commendable.
Before I resume my seat I should like to say once again that the staff of the public archives are most competent and courteous. While I do not believe the staff is large enough or that their facilities are adequate I would like to say on the basis of my personal experience over many years that they are, under the circumstances, doing a most excellent job and I commend their thoroughgoing devotion to the minister.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell us whether the historical collection which is to be found in the archives building on Sussex street comes under the estimates relating to the public archives?

Mr. Chairman, I did not catch the name of the collection. To what collection does the hon. gentleman refer?

The historical collection which takes up three or four rooms is the collection to which I referred. Does this come under the estimates for the public archives?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is quite correct.

I wish to say a few words about this collection. I think it is very important in that it is unfortunately the outward expression of the archives to the Canadian public. I believe there is perhaps a confusion of purpose in this building. I think archives are concerned with historical documents and should remain so. Perhaps the collection in the Sussex street building should concern itself with a display of documents from Canada's past in a tasteful and conservative-with a small "c"-way. In this way it would perhaps better serve its purpose than in its present form. At present a number of historical objects of an unrelated and incongruous nature are grouped together.
The national library and archives in Washington, D.C. provide a good example of what can be done in this field. I hope the minister will allow me to criticize in this area. I have supported other areas under her jurisdiction, and perhaps she will permit me to criticize this area. I have never seen a more incongruous or ill-assorted collection of paraphernalia in my life than exists in the historical collection on Sussex street. That was my impression on first visiting the building a few years ago with a group of young people. A historical collection with some kind of pattern, theme or continuity would make a better impression on the minds of young people than a confused collection. I realize that this is an infinitesimally small part of the work of the archives, and I appreciate the tremendous work that is being done in other areas of its jurisdiction including the work it does for scholars, but unfortunately the historical collection is what most Canadians see when they go on sightseeing tours in Ottawa.
For purposes of illustration let me refer to one of this group of rooms in the Sussex street building in which the historical collection is housed. In one room I found a replica of the Vimy war memorial, the colours of the militia of 1775 in an incredibly filthy case, a model section of Ottawa showing improvements-obviously the model was old and the improvements have been executed- a model of the parliament buildings, a model of a ship, the T.T.S. Lady Nelson, a model of a boat used in an Arctic exploration by Stefansson, a great mass of Indian and Eskimo material and a collection of photographs of early generals and lieutenant governors. There was absolutely no pattern whatever.


One of my colleagues has suggested that the collection comprises historical junk, but I would not go that far. I would say, however, that it does not give a clear picture of what the archives does. On the basis of a visit to the historical collection I am sure no young person would have any idea of the clarity that characterizes most of the work of the archives behind the facade of this confused historical collection.
It can be done. When I visited the archives I was interested to note an exhibit of Canada 200 years ago. There you have an example of a display which has a theme. You can follow this theme. You can see very clearly something of what Canada was in 1759, at the time of Wolfe and Montcalm and the siege of Quebec. I would bring this to the attention of the minister. I do not think the outward expression of the archives is of the best. I would hope that possibly something much more acceptable could be put forward to the public of Canada when they think of the Canadian public archives.

Mr. Chairman, possibly I can deal with the remarks of the hon. member for Peterborough first. The miscellaneous room to which he has referred is intended to touch upon names and events which are familiar to school children. Experience has shown that it is very successful for that purpose. The other room to which the hon. member has referred has been refitted. It had been intended to refit the first room, but it has been such a popular one that they have left it for the time being.
A number of comments were made here this morning, and I thank hon. members for the serious consideration which they have given to this subject.
With reference to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Port Arthur, I might say that the functions of the archives and the national library dovetail to a degree. That makes it quite natural that one person should head the two departments. Since I believe the hon. member has left a rather unfortunate impression with the committee I may say that no one has been more insistent on the need for an early start of the new building than the national librarian. I know the disappointment he feels over the fact that the building has not been made available with the required space. Owing to lack of space the library has not been able to begin the collection of periodicals and other serials on a large scale.
The other considerations which the hon, member mentioned are being kept carefully in mind by the national librarian, but I should tell him that no attempt at all is planned for a huge, all-inclusive, comprehensive library. As a matter of fact the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
national research council and the defence research board together, we feel, are filling adequately the needs of science. I may say we have watched the services of those two boards and considered the way in which techniques should be extended to the social science fields in particular with regard to the library. The national librarian is very well aware of that and of the complex body of materials referred to as documentation. I might just add that the library purchases consist almost entirely of reference works for a basic reference collection; that is, dictionaries, encyclopaedias, bibliographies, indexes, and so on.
Another field in which purchase has been made is that of books relating to Canada which are published abroad. Then there is a selection of current books published in Great Britain, France and the United States that appear to have fairly long term value for reference purposes. Special purchases are made when the opportunity offers, and I might mention a purchase of which we are very proud which was made recently, namely that of the Scholes music collection. As hon. members may know, this is a particularly fine nucleus for a music library, a collection made by Percy Scholes, who was not only a very fine musical scholar but a historian of note. We are most fortunate in having this collection in the national library.
In addition, I might just add that all our acquisitions do not come through purchase; many rare books and collections have come to the library either by request or gift. The Howe papers have been referred to by two hon. members. I might tell the committee that those papers are still the property of the estate at the present time, and although we have hopes, the conditions of access have not yet been determined. I do not know how many members of the committee realize that the archives is open 365 days of the year, 24 hours a day. Scholars may investigate to their hearts' content there, having made arrangements with the archives for research which they wish to do, at any hour of the day or night.
One other matter was touched upon, on which I should like to make comment. I refer to the comments with reference to establishing and making available service in the field of genealogy. This is a very expensive service, and most libraries and archives have had to curtail such service owing to the costs. At the present time the archives searches census returns up to 1871, old land records and early military records. 1 might add that the archives itself does thousands of searches every year.

The hon. lady said that I may have left or created an unfortunate impression. I think she must refer to the suggestion that because Dr. Lamb is not a librarian but is merely an archivist-that is, in the professional sense of the term-he has not pushed as hard for the national library as he might have. I am afraid this is an impression which I have encountered among some librarians, especially those at a distance from Ottawa. I would not like to feel that I left that impression, because I can just imagine it was quite a bit of heartbreak to Dr. Lamb when the national library was not proceeded with.
I should like to make a couple of comments upon the genealogy service. The minister has indicated briefly that it is a very expensive service. I am quite aware of this, and also of the fact that many people tend to think that if they fire off a letter to the government service or even to their member of parliament they should be entitled to a great deal gratis. I know I had a letter the other day from a man who evidently wanted me to provide him with publications totalling in value around $60 or $70. Evidently he just assumed that this was a government publication and that he could get it. But I think we must spell out more publicly, that is to say by way of public relations in the face of increasing demand, just what can be provided in genealogy terms because, with respect to so many people in Canada, once you get back several generations you have to move overseas. There should be some kind of attractive plan to make that type of publication available to our people who want to trace sources in England and in other countries in Europe from which so many Canadians seek their ethnic trail.
We have had a big hassle over the census form this year; we have incurred an expenditure of $170,000 to provide forms so that we can take care of the sensitivities of one group in this country, and it appears we may have outraged some of the feelings of another group. To answer the question in the form is going to require our chasing the ethnic trail on our fathers' side, and I know how difficult it is going to be; but the irony is that as Canada gets older and we become more stable, more and more people are going to be interested in tracing back their ancestry, and I just thought that in finding one's way through the maze of genealogy this particular agency, either the archives or the national library, would be able to give a great deal of help in at least setting out sign posts.
The minister has indicated that the national library is interested in documentation, and I should like to give a specific example. I have been bothered that the Canadian library association has to go before the Canada Council to get a grant to produce
2402	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the Canadian index, which I think the public archivist or national librarian will concede is a most important reference tool. I think he will also concede that it is typically Canadian and cannot be sold on any remunerative basis to cover the total expenses.
For the last several years it has been supported substantially by the Canada Council; yet we have been told by the head of the Canada Council, both the late Mr. Claxton and Dr. Trueman, that there is no intention on the part of the Canada Council to make this a continuing thing, that the set-up of the council is not such as to permit a whole block of its funds to be gradually nailed down for recurring expenses. This is a popular form of documentation and indexing, but it is immensely useful and at the same time there is no possibility of the service becoming selfsustaining. It is very much a public service.
What contribution can the national library make to this particular indexing; and, since this is a Canadian indexing service, why should it not be the kind of responsibility that the national library undertakes? In essence Canadiana is performing this function for the more permanent kind of publication and the Canadian index of periodicals is, of course, our means of keeping up to date with what is going on in all the periodical publishing fields in Canada. If the national library were to undertake this kind of chore, which seems to be properly within its function, I suggest that it should expand the index so that it will provide the kind of over-all service in the publications field that is not being provided at the present time by the Canadian library association.
The minister has said that the duties of archivist and national librarian dovetail very naturally. In an administrative sense this seems reasonable. I would assume that Dr. Lamb is primarily an administrator, but the point I was trying to make to the minister was that librarianship has become an extremely specialized field. In the field of documentation there is a complexity and a growing experimentation, I might say, in an effort to keep on top of records, and this is one of the outstanding developments of our times in the academic and research fields.
I suggest that the function of the archivist is much different, because archives by their very nature are confined in the main to records of the past and, in the present day, confined properly to public records of the past. While there are common problems in respect of cataloguing, indexing and control of these things, I suggest that librarianship has become more specialized, and that is why I personally feel that the whole field of librarianship would gain through having as


head of the national library a man who was a librarian and who was at the administrative pinnacle in that particular field.
The last point I wish to touch on in these remarks has to do with the suggestion of the minister that the conception of the national library collection has already been well worked out, and there is to be no overlapping in the field of science with the defence research board library or the national research council library. This is fine in that particular area, but I should like to know what is being done about the collections in other Ottawa offices. One of the problems that drives me up the wall as a user of the library of parliament is that when you go there and want a technical book on a specialized subject the library does not tend to have it. It has what I think is a pitiful collection in the economic field, particularly in connection with our resources in the field of forestry and allied fields. If you will take a ruler I think you will find that the books in the field of forestry cover 48 or 50 inches in the library of parliament. This is all the information that is available when we go looking for something to help us to deal with the problems that arise and try to help these industries.
This is all very well as a criticism of the library of parliament. You can go there and ask for a book in this particular field. They say that the forestry branch has an excellent library in this field and that they will get the material for you. I will concede that it does seem unreasonable to place within the library of parliament a specialized or extended collection on forestry and all these other fields for the use of maybe 265 members of parliament or a fraction thereof when just seven, eight or nine blocks away there is a magnificent, well indexed collection on forestry in a library staffed by people who know its contents intimately.
The very same criticism applies to the national library and its scope. Dotted across Ottawa we have these various government libraries. The economic research branch of the Department of Labour has a fairly extensive collection. In fact its collection in this field is a topnotch one. The Department of National Health and Welfare has a good collection. Fairly strong efforts are being made to keep these collections up to date and on a continuing basis, and to provide current reference service to the administrators. Service is also provided to the general public and members of parliament.
As a consequence of these departmental libraries in Ottawa, the spectrum of knowledge is fairly well covered. I will not say it is completely covered, but there is this coverage. What sort of overlapping are we likely to get in the national library? Is there

a plan to take much of the older material from these collections and put it in the national library? The minister suggested in her reply that the concentration was going to be in the field of social sciences. What does she mean by "social sciences"? Just how embracing is that? For example, is Canadian literary history a phase of social science? What kind of collection of novels is planned for the library? Is the library going to concentrate upon Canadian publications, or is it going to be concerned with the best that has been thought and said in the literary field?
I should like to know whether the national library is going to specialize in the collection of federal and provincial records and publications, or is it going to collect those of the commonwealth or of the world generally? Is it planned to have a supply of the "Congressional Record" on hand? Is the national library going to take over responsibility for the collection of all United Nations publications? I should like to have these questions answered in order to have some idea of the collection that is going to grow in the building we are going to have some day.

In answer to a couple of the comments of the hon. member, I might say that ever since the library came into existence in 1952 it has published the Canadian index of periodicals and documentary films. I think the hon. member regretted that there was no such publication available. It has been published every year.
Not by the national library.

Yes, by the national
library.
The Canadian index of periodicals?
The annual Canadian index of periodicals and documentary films has been published every year by the national library since 1952, when the library first came into existence.
What publication is it that is issued by the Canadian library association and supported by the Canada Council?

The Canadian library
association compiles and puts out monthly mimeographed editions. The national library puts these together into a comprehensive index which is an accumulation of the monthly editions.

While I am concerned with the Canada Council paying a considerable part of the cost for this particular service, my question was directed to why this cost was not taken over completely by the national library. I am sorry I missed recognition of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that part so far as the cumulative publication is concerned, but I realize, as I am sure the minister does, that the main cost concerns the actual indexing proportion. The cumulative portion is mainly printing, and the charge is not great. If it is not the case that a very large contribution is being made by the national library, I would like to know how much more it would cost for the national library to take over this complete service.

I cannot make an estimate of the additional cost. This is a matter that can be considered and possibly will have to be considered one of these days, but at the present time the information is not available. This whole problem covers a wide field involving many considerations, and I do not think that in a short space of time I can enumerate them all. If the hon. member would like a report in this regard I would be glad to have one prepared.
I might add also, with reference to his comments regarding the information being scattered around, that it is all catalogued, as he probably knows, in the union catalogue which is the key to all the libraries and the books therein. I was wondering as a result of some of the remarks the hon. member made whether he has ever visited the national library.

Mr. Chairman, the reason I would like to know very definitely the role the national library thinks it should play is that we are going to have the Canada Council before the public accounts committee in a few weeks, and I feel that the Canada Council is trying to keep its recurring expenditures and grants as low as possible. If it is seriously considered that the national library could fill this role, it would then follow that there would be more Canada Council money available for scholarships and other things.

I think the best solution to this problem is for the hon. member to consult the national librarian. I understand he has never done that. If he would make an appointment to call on the national librarian I am sure he would be glad to supply the hon. member with the information that is available, and I am sure this would serve his purposes.

The minister made the point that I had never consulted the national librarian. There are a tremendous number of people whom I think all members of parliament would like to consult, but it is very difficult to get around to them all. I feel that members make an attempt to focus their attention on questions and suggestions in so far as the expenditures are concerned, and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I suppose primarily we should be interested in cutting them down. I was not trying to suggest, as my earlier comments will show, what in effect might be a cutting down of the whole thing by creating a grand institutional library. I am quite pleased to hear that this is not being conceived. If I can break it down more particularly to Ottawa libraries, I know there is a union catalogue; I also know that libraries are growing all the time, and that union catalogues go out of date. It is a large job keeping them up to date.
The hon. member is quite wrong. This catalogue is kept up to date all the time.

Yes, I know that the catalogue is kept up to date all the time, but I was going on to say that this takes considerable time on the part of the librarians both in regard to storing the books and in having the index prepared. What I am trying to get from the minister, and I would appreciate a statement from her not at this time but in the future perhaps in letter form, is how the libraries in the public service in Ottawa are going to dovetail in with the national library. I am not speaking in terms of a catalogue that will be kept by the national librarian, but in terms of the actual coverage and placing of books. Because we have a national health and welfare library, will everything in that field be primarily the responsibility of that department and not that of the national library except in so far as indexing or cataloguing is concerned? Will this also apply to the Department of Justice library in the supreme court building, which I understand tends to be a growing one? I would like to know what the liaison is in this field which prevents duplication.
The point that intrigues me is that if these departmental libraries build up their collections in a good way, as I assume most of them are doing, they finally will reach the stage of competition with the national library in terms of its collection because, as I suggested earlier, the government of Canada in its libraries is covering almost the whole spectrum of publications except perhaps in the literary or historical field.
Item agreed to.

speechtext: That completes the estimates for which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is responsible. We now go to the Department of Agriculture, vote No. 1. This vote will be found on page 4 of the blue book; the details are on page 93.

Administration branch-
1. Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $991,098.

Mr. Chairman, in presenting the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the fiscal year 1961-62 I should like to point out that the summary and the details of services reflect certain organizational changes which have taken place.
During the past year responsibility for the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners was transferred to the Minister of Agriculture. Also during the year the forest biology division of the research branch was transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Forestry. The total to be voted to the Department of Agriculture in these estimates is $122,202,953. This includes the amount required for the board of grain commissioners, which is $6.5 million.
There is, of course, no estimate provision for the Canadian wheat board. However, the amounts shown as authorized by statute include $49 million for payment of carrying costs under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and $920,000 for the provision of interest free cash advances to western grain producers. These items were previously carried in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The amount to be voted, plus that authorized by statute, comes to a total of $172,181,953. The corresponding figure for 1960-61, as shown on page 2, is $205.7 million.
This latter includes the figure for the present fiscal year for the board of grain commissioners for carrying costs of wheat reserves and for advance grain payments. It does not include the amount voted in 1960-61 for the forest biology division. The amounts and details shown for 1961-62 and 1960-61 are therefore drawn on a comparable basis and reflect the requirements for and expenditures on the activities now conducted under the Department of Agriculture.
The committee may be interested in a broad break-down of the $122.2 million among the main categories of departmental activities. The amount required for research is $28.8 million, which is 24 per cent of the total. The administration of legislation requires $32.4 million, or 28 per cent of the total. This covers the wide range of legislation administered by the department, including the grading of farm products, animal and plant health, the Canada Grain Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act. For rehabilitation, which includes P.F.R.A. in western Canada and

M.M.R.A. in the maritimes, $27.2 million is required. This is 22 per cent of the total. Grants and subsidies require $31.2 million, which is 25 per cent of the total.
The main item in this category is freight assistance on western feed grains, for which $20 million is provided. Included in this category also are quality premium payments on hogs and cheese, lime assistance, grants to fairs and exhibitions and to agricultural organizations. The balance of the vote, some $2.6 million, is required for departmental administration, which includes the economics division.
The committee will note that the amount to be voted in these estimates is $40.5 million less than that granted for the 1960-61 fiscal year. The figure for the present fiscal year, however, includes supplementary estimates to date, the largest item in which was the $42 million for western grain producers' acreage payments. Excluding that amount, these estimates show an increase of $1.5 million over the amount provided for the year ending on March 31.
It will be noted in the details that there are increases in some votes and decreases in others. The largest category of increases is for salaries, which are higher by $7.6 million, due mostly to increases in salary rates. The actual staff increase provided for next year is the equivalent of 73 positions, which is six tenths of 1 per cent of the present staff total. The next largest increase, of almost $2 million, is in the vote for construction of works under land rehabilitation. This is accounted for by greater activity in the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. In fact $2.6 million more will be required for that project in 1961-62 than was required in 1960-61.
I may say that construction of the dam is proceeding at a satisfactory pace, and on schedule. Stage 1 of the embankment has been completed and stage 2 is nearing completion. Work is proceeding on the downstream diversion tunnels. Contracts will be let shortly for the upstream diversion tunnels and for stage 3 of the embankment.
I think I need not take the time of the committee at this stage to go into details of individual items of expenditure. I know that many hon. members of the committee will be interested enough to discuss these subjects under the respective votes. I do wish to say a word about farm income. In any analysis of farm income in recent years it soon becomes apparent that after the war we were in what can be described as a sellers' market. This was the period of reconstruction in Europe; this was the period of the Korean war. Since about 1953, and possibly starting with the calendar year 1954, we have entered
Supply-Agriculture
into a buyers' market. Our Canadian industry and Canadian farmers are now faced more than ever before with the crash of competition.
I thought the committee might be interested in seeing just how we were making out in increasing farm income in this period of the buyers' market, or this competitive period which we are now in. I have put together some figures obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics. These figures give total cash income, which does include supplementary payments by the federal government.
I am going to read these figures by calendar years. Perhaps some hon. members will wish to copy them down, so I will read them slowly enough for that to be done. In 1954 the total cash income was $2,378 billion; in 1955 it was $2,384 billion; in 1956 it was $2,647 billion; in 1957 it was $2,575 billion. If one adds these figures together and works out the average, the average total cash income for farmers in Canada for those four years, the first four years of the buyers' market, comes to $2,493 billion. The figure for 1958 was $2,873 billion; the figure for 1959 was $2,808 billion; the figure for 1960, which is not yet final from the D.B.S., was $2,861 billion. If you add the last three figures you will find that the average total cash income for each of those years was $2,847 billions.
Therefore the conclusion which can be derived from this analysis is that during each of those three calendar years there was an increase in the total cash income to the farmers of Canada amounting to more than $350 million. I think this does indicate in some measure the efforts of the government not only to stabilize farm income but to increase it.
May I ask a question at this point? Does the minister have any figures or statistics showing the increases in the cost of production over the same period of time?

I will deal with that later on when I deal with net income.
The full picture cannot be appreciated until we examine how many farmers there are. There has been a steady decline in the farm population for many years now, so I will give the figures of the number of farmers and then relate them to income. In 1954, in round figures, there were 594,000 farmers in Canada. In 1955 there were 584,000; in 1956,
575.000	and in 1957, 565,000. If you average the number of farmers in those four calendar years the figure comes to approximately
580.000	during that four-year period of the buyers' market. In 1958 the number of farmers is estimated at 555,000. In 1959 the figure is
546.000	and in 1960, 536,000. If you average the number of farmers during that three-year period the figure is approximately 545,000.

Supply-Agriculture
Now, if one takes the average number of farmers in the first four years of this seven-year period of the buyers' market and divides this income among those farmers, the figure of cash income for the years 1954 to 1959 inclusive is $4,303. If one takes the numbers of farmers for the three-year period 1958 to 1960 inclusive and divides the income for the same period among those farmers, the income per farm comes to $5,214. Therefore, comparing the four-year period 1954-57 with the three-year period 1958-60, there is an increase in cash income amounting to $911 per farmer.
It is obvious that this increase in cash income per farm is due, first of all, to the efforts which we have been making to increase farm income and, second, to the fact that there is a smaller number of farmers. By placing these two sets of figures in juxtaposition one can draw, I think, fairly sound conclusions.
Having put on record those figures which deal with total cash income, I should like now to deal with this question which has puzzled farmers for 25 years, namely why it is that farmers do not receive what they call a fair share of the national income. It is not too easy to find some group in our economy which is comparable with the farmers. The only group I can find which seems to give us some basis of comparison comprises those who are engaged in unincorporated non-farm business. So, from the dominion bureau of statistics labour force survey, I am going to put some figures on the record which I think will show how we are making out in our deliberate policy of seeing what we can do to bring farm income up to a fair share of the national income.
The figures I intend to quote now are net farm returns per farm. In 1954 the figure was $1,792. In 1955 it was $2,376. In 1956 it was $2,836, and in 1957 it was $2,133. Adding and averaging, one gets a figure which shows that during this four-year period of the buyers' market the net income of farmers was $2,284. But one should compare this with the income of non-farm unincorporated business. In 1954 non-farm incorporated business received, on the average, $2,883. In 1955 the figure was $3,162; in 1956, $3,341; in 1957, $3,351. The average for this period received by non-farm unincorporated business was $3,184 as compared with $2,284 by the farmers. Put as a percentage of farm income, and relating this to the net income of the non-farm unincorporated group, the farmers received 71.7 per cent of the income received by a reasonably comparable group.
Looking at the figures for the years 1958 and 1959, net farm income in 1958 was $2,891 and in 1959, $2,643. Naturally, we have no

figures yet for 1960 and we shall not have those figures for some time, but those two years I mentioned give an average of $2,767. Non-farm income has been increasing as well in the last two years. In 1958 it was $3,563 and in 1959 it was $3,619, or an average for those two calendar years of $3,591. Expressing these figures as a percentage of net farm income, as related to non-farm income, the percentage for the last two years is 77 per cent. Therefore during the last two calendar years of the buyers' market as compared with the four previous years of the buyers' market, farm income as a percentage of nonfarm income for a comparable group has risen from 71.7 per cent to 77 per cent.
I have been looking at the figures for the first three quarters of 1960. I suggest that when the figures are finally calculated for the calendar year 1960 they will reflect this same upward trend in percentage. Therefore, even though the gradual gain in farm net income as compared with non-farm net income is obvious, it indicates that at the rate we are going it will take about ten years to bring farm net income up to the same percentage level of non-farm income. I put these figures on the record to make clear just one fact, that I do believe we are closing the gap, and this was our intention.
I think it is necessary for me to point out that when one analyses the farm income of this country product by product and region by region, it soon becomes clear that the most variable area is the prairie province area. It soon becomes clear also that the most variable commodities in rate of return are the grain products of western Canada. Therefore it is clear that any government in charge of the selling of wheat, oats and barley has as a first duty to press forward in every way possible to increase the sales of western grain.
I need not tell a committee composed of hon. members knowledgeable with respect to the relationship of eastern and western agriculture that if western Canadian grain is not sold in export markets, the pressure on farmers in every part of the country grows. Therefore it is in the interests of farmers in every part of Canada to closely examine the efforts of the government in the selling of grain in the export market. I do not intend to make any predictions as to what the final total sales will be during this crop year, but I do intend to say something about the efforts we are making to sell grain. I am of the opinion that a good deal of credit goes to my colleague, the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, for the efforts he made through the wheat board in making direct contact with our main customers and in moving into what I call the new market areas

to establish the preliminary contacts to make known the type of wheat we have and its particular qualities that would be an advantage to those countries if they used it. This means there has to be a concerted sales effort. In addition to the general approach of the salesman, we must have a concentrated attack on all the problems that are associated with the selling of this product.
It has become very obvious, I believe, that if we are to continue to sell our flour and wheat in some areas of the world we are going to have to exert every effort at all levels to establish flour mills in those countries and provide the bakeries and demonstration units that must be associated with them to get the maximum consumption of bread in countries that have not used bread before.
We are in full course on this program. It is not going to be easy, because we have competitors in the sale of grain all around the world who have the same idea. We have individual promoters in various countries that are actively seeking the same type of opportunity as individuals or groups. However, it will be of interest, I know, for the committee to be aware that we are in full course on this policy ourselves.
Another point I should like to mention in this connection is that it is now very obvious that there are other things for which wheat can be utilized besides the traditional product, bread. It is no secret that thousands of years ago wheat and barley were used as a staple diet not in the form of bread. In many countries of the world where the tendency to turn to the use of the new product, bread, is slow, it might be possible for us to sell wheat ready for human consumption closer to the natural form.
I want to close off in the next few minutes after making known to the committee what we are doing with respect to another aspect *of our sales efforts. Starting January 1 we set up under the Canadian wheat board a technical services and market research division, the objectives of which are as follows:
1.	To assess at first hand the raw material requirements of the wheat consuming industries in all the potential and actual wheat importing areas of the world.
2.	Where it appears likely that Canadian wheat or flour may be used to advantage in such markets, to work with the consumer industries to the end that they become aware of the advantages that can accrue from the use of such wheat or flour. In areas where the consuming industries are already adequately aware of the advantages offered by the use of Canadian wheat, to maintain close liaison with industrial and government technical personnel to ensure the maximum dis-
Supply-Agriculture
semination of technical information and know how, concerning Canadian wheat and flour.
3.	To establish and maintain technical liaison in the areas of grain handling, wheat breeding, quality assessment and milling and baking in those countries which export wheat, or which could become exporters of wheat, of a type potentially competitive with any of the various grades of Canadian wheat.
4.	To establish liaison with government officials and scientific personnel in underdeveloped countries which might develop in time a bread eating habit. To offer assistance, in these areas, in the establishment of cereal laboratories and in setting up quality criteria.
5.	To write, edit, translate and publish such bulletins, pamphlets, press releases, etc., as appear useful in support of the objectives listed under item 2.
At the head of this new division we have a topnotch cereal chemist, a young man. We have as his assistant an expert on Canadian milling. Serving under them will be four or five younger men with multilanguage ability who will learn the techniques of Canadian milling and the chemical properties of our grain and will be able to deal directly with these countries in their own language to make our present and potential customers aware of how they can use Canadian wheat to better advantage. I think this is the type of thing a corporation would do in selling its products through familiarizing the consumers with the best uses of the products it has available.
I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman, for allowing me to run over the normal hour of adjournment for a few minutes. If hon. members will bear with me for another few seconds I will conclude these remarks.
I cannot, as Minister of Agriculture, let this occasion pass without expressing to the committee and to the country my deep concern and anxiety over what would happen to our growing wheat export sales if there were a major rail strike at a critical time during the movement of grain to tidewater, particularly on the west coast. The consequences to the western farmer would be nothing short of catastrophic. I appeal to labour and to management to approach their responsibilities in the full realization of the public interest involved.

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks made before the lunch recess by

In the field of agriculture, as well as in the fields of trade, finance, taxes, unemployment and several others, the over-all situation is such that the farmers are losing confidence in their government and, what is more serious still, are losing confidence in their profession. Who would not lose confidence after the fabulous promises made in 1957 and in 1958 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his candidates when comparing them to the actual facts?
We recall the promises made during the 1957 campaign by the Prime Minister himself when he said in Toronto:
We shall provide farmers with their fair share of the national income by a price support policy for farm products which will be related to cost prices.
And he added:
(Text):
Parity not charity.

(Translation):
During the 1957 session, which preceded the 1958 election, the government saw fit to introduce a bill aiming at the passage of an act for the stabilization of the price of agricultural commodities.
The preamble of that act was of course very promising; it read as follows:
Whereas it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income:
Therefore, the government-
However, after the 1958 election, we saw the government repudiate its promises. Here is the evidence. When, on February 23, 1960, the Liberals moved a non-confidence motion which was in accordance with the preamble of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, 172 Conservative members voted against the motion. In doing that, they voted against their own legislation, against the principles incorporated in that legislation the object of which was to provide farmers with their fair share of the national income.

Mr. Chairman, I will now give figures which do not tally with the ones presented by the Minister of Agriculture this morning, although they are from the dominion bureau of statistics. I quote:

As a matter of fact the cost to the Canadian taxpayers for meeting the commitments under the farm legislation was $77 million in 1960, $22.1 million in 1959 and $60.1 million in 1958.

Moreover, while the farmers were receiving less for their products, they were not paying less for the commodities and services they bought.

How many times have we heard that the Conservative government would give the farmers the share of Canada's wealth to the production of which they co-operated?
But what is even more serious is the fact that the government and more particularly the Department of Agriculture has just announced in the farm review for January 1961, that the 1961 income would remain at the 1960 level.
When will this government keep its promises? When will it give parity, not charity? When will it put back in each farmer's pocket the $120 that the Liberal government took from him in taxes each year?
Now, I should like to quote what the Minister of Agriculture stated recently to a group of dairy farmers of Canada at a meeting held in Vancouver.
I want to quote these few words to show how the statements of the Minister of Agriculture in this house can differ from the ones he makes elsewhere.
Here is what he said:
(Text):
The purposes are, first of all to take out the ups and downs and to stabilize prices; the second purpose, in so far as products consumed in Canada are concerned, is to use this as a platform on which we can begin to build up the returns to agriculture so as to give them a fair share of
