the national income or, in other words, moving towards parity of income. This is not charity- this is using the legislative power to give the farmer some of the protection that the other segments of the economy have had. You all know what I am talking about.
The working man has the protection of provincial legislation which sets the minimum wage. He has the protection of the tariff for the goods that he produces for the home market. He has the protection of unions if he works in an organized industry where the union bargains to make sure that he gets his share of the national income. The farmer has not got this kind of help. Mr. Chairman, I would now like to address myself to the situation of feed grain deliveries in the eastern areas during the summer, until the closing of navigation. We learned in the newspapers that from August to the end of the navigation season, in the harbours of Montreal, Quebec city, Baie Comeau and others, a number of ships were waiting in line for two, three and even four weeks in front of elevators full of grain, particularly wheat for export. Those ships could not unload their cargoes, and there was no feed grain on the eastern markets.
In the meantime, our farmers were having all sorts of difficulties in getting supplies, and when they could get them they had to pay a high premium. Now, this shortage of feed grain on the eastern markets, was due to a decision of the Canadian wheat board to ship only export grades to eastern ports. Incredible losses of the order of $1,000 to $3,000 daily were suffered by ship owners, not to mention the loss suffered by farmers

who saw their operating costs increase on account of the higher prices they had to pay for their feed grain.
Although the oats crop will be considerably increased this year over last year, the Canadian wheat board charged 84J cents a bushel for October oats, compared with 60 cents a bushel paid to western producers, at Fort William.
The feed grain requirements in the eastern areas amount to more than a hundred million bushels a year; and from October to the end of the navigation season, close to 50 million bushels must be shipped to fill the requirements for the winter months. There is not much publicity about this 100 million bushel eastern market, but when a few million bushels are sold abroad, the publicity machine of the Department of Agriculture starts rolling at once. Because of the lack of interest shown by the Canadian wheat board and the government, the eastern farmers will have to pay $300 more per carload for moving their grain than it would have cost them if that grain had been moved by ship at the proper time.
Another consequence the farmers will have to bear will be the one resulting from the discriminatory policy carried out by the board and the government since a decision was made last December 28. May I recall the words used by the Prime Minister himself in a speech made in his home town of Prince Albert, when he said: "From now on, the western mills may also buy their oats, barley and wheat in their own provinces, directly and on the open market, at lower prices than those asked by the board for the domestic market in the east."
Unfortunately for the eastern farmers, he stressed the fact that his government was not taking any position which might be the slightest cause of trouble for the board.
With these words, the Prime Minister gave a blank cheque to the grain mill owners, allowing them to organize for integration. Indeed, with the considerable amounts which they have at their disposal, they will build chicken ranches, pig farms and even packing plants and ultimately take over from the farmers in this country. Then, they will be able to pay their own price for their grain without considering the wheat board or the grain producers.
It is strange that the prairie farmers, who always supported the Canadian wheat board,

should have asked for an authorization to sell their grain without being subjected to the regulations of the board. Since then, they get prices 50 per cent lower than they were getting through the board. Today, they are selling their surplus to the grain mills, to other elevators, to other livestock producers, or else they have to increase the number of their animals to use up their grain.
I should like at this point to deal with two particular areas of the province of Quebec which are affected by feed grain prices, the lake St. John and Chicoutimi areas.
I deplore the fact that the hon. members for those two regions are not in the house to learn of the situation which prevails there.
There are not many Liberal members in the house at this time.
This matter should also be of interest to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), and yet he is absent.

Mr. Chairman, Canada's subsidy legislation contains rules that are detrimental to certain regions. I will explain how that is so.
To show the difference in transportation costs paid by the farmers who buy grain, I have chosen two points equally distant from Quebec city.
A freight rates analysis shows that the rate between Quebec and Roberval, a distance of 188 miles, is 36 cents. On the other hand, for the same distance, or almost-189 miles -from Quebec to Bic, the rate is 32 cents during summer and 42 cents during winter, or an average of 37 cents.
At this time, the rates between Roberval and Quebec, and Bic and Quebec are identical, to a cent or so, but when we take the grants that are paid towards grain transportation, we notice that the Roberval area receives 43 cents per hundredweight while the Bic people get 67 cents in summer and 68 cents in winter.
Mr. Chairman, that enables us to see the difference between the grain rates in two areas equally distant from Quebec city, and it shows that the lake St. John farmers are at a disadvantage.
Mr. Chairman, I could quote other figures for the towns of Normandin and Mont Joli, which are located respectively at 219 miles and 217 miles from Quebec city, as well as

figures for Chicoutimi and Mont Joli which are located respectively at 228 miles and 217 miles from Quebec city.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the minister should make a survey of the freight rates and tell us in a not too distant future what he intends to do in order to give justice to the lake St. John and Chicoutimi farmers.
In fact, those farmers should be treated on the same basis as those of the rest of the province of Quebec.
The farmers in both these areas have accepted huge sacrifices to remain on the agricultural map of the province of Quebec. They have kept abreast of technological advance, improved their farms, set up cooperatives, and particularly a co-operative packing plant which made it possible to process on the spot meats to be distributed in the area. They have invested millions of dollars, and if their situation does not improve soon, it will become untenable.
It is only with great efforts and sacrifices that those farmers have been able to establish organizations which are the pride of the area.
If they are to preserve the millions of dollars invested in their organizations, it is logical that the government play its part now and treat those farmers in the same way it treats the other farmers in the province.
What I feel can fairly be asked on behalf of the farmers in the province of Quebec is this:

by the present Minister of Agriculture, and its manner of delivery, as compared with those made by the long term minister of agriculture of the former administration. This morning, the Minister of Agriculture spoke in quiet and deliberate terms. The former minister of agriculture, of course, always spoke in a very loud voice, with great energy and with a glass of water in his hand. Which former minister?

I am referring to the minister of agriculture in the former administration. I said "the long term minister in the former administration", and I referred to the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. As for the present Minister of National Defence, I would not wish to go over the experience he had as minister of agriculture, but he was not a water drinker. The present Minister of Agriculture used a great many statistics this morning. The former minister, the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, was a master in the use of statistics and he used a great number of them whenever he spoke. But I think the present minister has put the former minister to shame. I think my friend Jimmie Gardiner would look like a backrow student who had just entered kindergarten compared with a professional like the present Minister of Agriculture as far as the use of statistics is concerned.
One would never think this was a minister speaking for the Conservative party which used to talk in such eloquent terms about parity prices, a fair share of the national income and an improvement of the farmer's position, or that he was the spokesman for a party which used to talk so eloquently on behalf of the small farmer. Now things have changed. What we got from the Minister of Agriculture when he opened these important estimates was not a review of the government's agricultural policy nor a projection of the prospects for agriculture in the years to come but, rather, a discouraging review of very deplorable conditions in this industry. The most significant figures which the minister used, in my opinion, were those which reflected the decline in the number of agricultural operators and they showed how quickly the small farmer is being pushed to the wall under this administration, as he was under the former administration.
I was surprised that the present Minister of Agriculture did not review this thing which they used to call the farmers' charter of rights, known about the country as Bill

237, under which farmers were to get this parity of income and receive by way of deficiency payment technique the kind of support prices for which they have been asking for so many years.
On a point of order, the hon. member for Assiniboia has used two terms-"pushed to the wall" and "parity prices". I should like to have definitions of those two terms.

Under this great charter of agricultural rights the farmer has not been faring well, and I think it was significant that the Minister of Agriculture did not refer in his discourse this morning to the effect of the prices stabilization act upon the prices which have been paid to the farmer. I was, of course, for many years a sharp critic of Mr. Gardiner because the average prices established under this legislation were not payable, as some of us felt they should be, directly to the producer, or they were not guaranteed to the producer. Instead, they were paid to the packing companies and the farmer had to deal with the packing companies and do what he could to get from them the established floor. The deficiency payment technique has provided little assistance to agriculture producers because there is no certainty about the way in which the legislation operates. There is no certainty that a farmer who receives less than the stated average national price will recover his losses. As a matter of fact, his chances of recovering those losses are very poor indeed. No deficiency payment has been made in respect of hogs, yet in at least three months, February, March and April, prices less than the stated national average were received by producers who marketed hogs in those months and such people have in fact incurred a very distinct loss which they have no hope of recovering.
This type of so-called support has been used in connection with the marketing of eggs and as in this field I suggest it has been a very dismal failure from the standpoint of the producer. If, as the present Minister of National Defence used to say, one of the purposes of this type of support was to reduce production at times when there appeared to be a surplus, then it has been successful. producers and by providing nowhere near the national average price for all the eggs farmers have sold.

There have been some agreeable indications in recent days of additional sales of wheat being made to certain countries of the world. These are welcome and I hope these additions to our regular markets may be maintained.

Because of the famine condition and the attitude of the United States with respect to the sale of commodities to that country, Canada was successful in making sales in that market. I am pleased about those sales, but a great deal more must be done to bring about increased grain sales if we are to have any hope of adequate sales on a longer term basis. What is our surplus of barley?

The minister said the situation was not satisfactory. This year it is even less satisfactory than last year in terms of our accomplishments to this point.
It has been said, and I think accurately, that grain is sold through what might be called a pipe line and that in order that a producer at the extreme end of the pipe line may feed his grain through, the grain obviously must come out at the other end. Farmers' marketings are reflected with some variations in the quotas that prevail. The quotas prevailing in western Canada today leave much to be desired.

Thanks to the grain
handlers' strike.

The minister knows as well as I do, and perhaps even better, that his area has suffered in the past with respect to delivery quotas. His constituency and mine are on the apex of deliveries, as it were. In some years we cannot take advantage of the eastern deliveries and in others we cannot take advantage of the western deliveries; we have to wait to the last. This has been difficult for producers in our part of western Canada.
The farmers' union has put forward a substantial point deserving of consideration by the minister. They ask that there be a guaranteed quota delivery. The guarantee should be such that if the wheat board is unable to take delivery by the end of the crop year then the difference could be paid

to the producer for the grain on his farm. If an 8-bushel quota were guaranteed, as was requested, and a farmer at a given point could market only a 6-bushel quota the board should be prepared to buy the difference on the farm in the farmer's storage. The board could then take its own good time in moving out the grain in the days ahead. By this method some equality would be established in the marketing of grain. I suggest that equality is needed and is long overdue.

Did we not
equalize the quotas last year?
They were not too bad last year. The marketings were not equalized but less damage was done last year by this method than on former occasions, and I was very pleased to see some improvement.

speechtext: Improvement under a Conservative government.

The hottest issue at the moment, as far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned, is this whole question of the government having allowed the feed mills in western Canada legally to buy grain at bankrupt prices and to go into a system of stealing, in a legal way, a substantial part of the farmer's normal returns from grain. I feel that this action has amounted to an abdication of principle. It has been a great mistake. Ninety eight per cent of the farmers will lose the chance to deliver this amount of grain through a quota system. The fact that 98 per cent of the farmers will not be marketing grain to the feed mills means that greater pressure will be placed upon them to go into the livestock business to an increasing extent. This means-and there is no argument about this-that the total income of western producers from grain will be lost because the prices paid by the feed mills in western Canada today are lower than the wheat board prices, and in some instances the final prices are disgracefully low.
The minister has promised to take a look at this. I hope he will take a thorough look at it, and I express the strong hope that this mistake will be corrected in the next marketing year. After all, the excuse for doing this has been that the wheat board could not police its quotas. The actions of the wheat board were upheld by the courts. The Supreme Court of Canada said that the wheat board had the right to police its quota for all mills, agreement, mills and non-agreement mills. Once the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the wheat board this government in effect repudiated the decision of the courts by saying, we are changing the rules and the feed mills will be allowed "legally" to get this grain at bootleg prices.

Undoubtedly, this has been a severe blow to the system of orderly marketing of grain. What happened in the committee this afternoon spelled out exactly what I feared would happen. In the committee this afternoon no less a person that the official agricultural spokesman for the official opposition said it was his opinion that the grain going to feed mills in eastern Canada should be removed from wheat board control. The pressure that goes with this position taken by the official opposition, together with the natural desire of people in eastern Canada to get their grain at the lowest possible price, suggests that those of us who said this was the thin edge of the wedge that would lead to greater pressure being placed on the government to open the door much wider have been proven correct.
I am disappointed with the stand taken by the Liberal party. I think the official stand they have taken today has been a great mistake. They had better have a caucus and take another look at this subject because the people whom I represent will not be happy to learn that the position of the Liberal party opens the door-
May I ask the hon. member a question?

When I finish the hon. member may ask all the questions he likes.
I appreciate the reasons given for this action, but I think the sooner we return to the position of ensuring that the wheat board quota regulations shall be enforced on all mills in all parts of Canada the better it will be for the Canadian producer and for everyone concerned in this field.
I had hoped the government would tell us today what they were going to do to improve the income position of the farmer. I was curious to learn from the minister whether it was the intention of the government once again to pay the $1 an acre to farmers in the west, amounting to $40 million or $42 million. I would be interested in knowing whether the government intends to change the method by which this payment is made, if it is going to be made, and put it on the unit system, but there was no comment on that.
The Minister of Agriculture wound up his remarks by giving it as his opinion that a railway strike would place the agricultural producers of Canada in a very difficult position. He called on railway and management to do everything possible to avert a strike. I agree with the minister's statements. I suggest that one of the main reasons we are in this position today is the failure of the government to do anything last fall, except procrastinate and postpone the trouble. They

said, "We will not settle it in December; we will postpone it until May 16 and then we shall have to settle it all over again," or the railways can go to the board of transport commissioners and get another hike in freight rates which are already too high.
I think the minister might have singled out management a little more in his remarks. The railway workers said, "We will accept the conciliation board report". I cannot speak for them, but I would not be at all surprised if they would accept the report today if the management of the railway companies were prepared to do the same. The minister lumps them together, although it was the railway companies which refused to settle on the basis of the conciliation board report.
Do you always support that policy?

The government has a great responsibility to deal with the agricultural situation. I suggest that to do that these steps should be taken.
First, the government should exert every effort to move the surplus of grain within this country to the markets of the world and to the people who need it.
Second, the government, instead of weakening the orderly system of marketing, should maintain it and expand it.
Third, the government should give every help and assistance to the development of the co-operative movement in Canada at the producer and consumer level, a movement that I think can be of great service to the agricultural producers. To this end I would suggest that, at least for a beginning a co-operative branch should be set up in the Department of Agriculture to lend encouragement to the co-operatives in Canada.
Fourth, I suggest that it is time the government defined its income supports for agricultural producers and spelled out just how and what it is going to do to fulfil its commitments to Canadian producers that would provide them with a fair share of the national income.

Will the hon. member permit a question? I did not have much luck with my questions to the official agricultural spokesman for the Liberal party. Perhaps the last speaker knows a little bit more about agriculture. He has deplored the falling grain markets in western Canada. Unfortunately for him he mentioned barley. I should like to ask the hon. member if he recalls that the province of Alberta, and Saskatchewan to some degree, lost a market for pearling barley in the Orient by virtue of a strike of longshoremen on the Pacific coast which was fully supported and ardently advocated by his party.
Mr. Chairman, that statement is another lie. It is a real lie.

You endorsed it.

That is not true either. That is another statement that is completely false. Mr. Chairman, my first remarks must be, of course, to express my satisfaction and that of the people I represent with the upward trend in both gross and net farm income. The people in the area I represent are quite pleased with the trend and I think they will continue to be pleased. Like the minister, I sincerely hope for a stay in the trend of farm population away from the farms, and I think the efforts of the government are wholly bent in that direction.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska has referred to some promises made with regard to farmers and farm incomes and so on in the campaigns in 1957 and 1958. I should like to refer to some more recent promises made not by members of the government but made at the so-called great national Liberal rally. I should like to refer to the Country Guide for February, 1961. In that issue there is an article with a headline in red, naturally, reading, "Buying the Vote". The article reads in part as follows:
The Liberal rally held in Ottawa early last month may have made the party faithful who were present glow with enthusiasm, but on at least two counts it was a sad performance .. .
From an agricultural standpoint, the Liberal rally seemed to be completely bewildered and without inspiration. Mr. Pearson accused the Diefenbaker government of "failure to produce any kind of a solution for agricultural problems". Well, if the Liberals think what came out of the rally resolutions is a better guide to success than what is currently being offered, they are badly mistaken ... Promising western grain growers a parity price on their first 300 bushels of deliveries each year is not an answer to the grain problem.

The article goes on to say:
Let no one misunderstand us. We are not opposed to social advancement on a wide front, either in agriculture or other sectors of our society.
On the other hand, they do not believe in offering something which is impossible of performance. The hon. member also mentioned rather scornfully, I thought, the wheat sales which have just been completed. I might say for his information that the farmers of western Canada were very highly elated at these additional sales. He did not tell us, of course, what the relative figures were of surpluses of feed grains compared with wheat. I suggest that he should look up these figures. He will find that we do not have a surplus of feed grain but we do have a rather large surplus of wheat.
With reference to the stand of the official opposition with respect to agriculture, I go back to something which was said by "farmer Paul" as he was referred to in the Ottawa Journal last fall. The article in the Journal reads in part as follows:
Mr. Martin, beaming at the government benches as he concluded a speech, said that he might have made mistakes here and there. "I will pit my zeal and my desire"-
He said it smilingly, of course.

"to do something to assist the western farmer against what my hon. friend promised and has failed to do."
I do not look upon the efforts in recent weeks as evidence of failure when we sell over 50 million bushels of grain. In "Ottawa Report" of February 14, 1961, prepared for the Thompson publications, the hon. member for Essex East is also referred to as the "wicked fairy and his mother goose tales". I think the description is very apt.
1 was rather amazed to hear the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska speak about direct half-price sales of grain without quotas to the feed mills. I wondered whether he got his figures from the hon. member for Assiniboia or from the Martin bureau of statistics.
Don't blame me for his figures.
In this regard I should like to refer to certain information which appeared in a newspaper recently. The prices are given that were being paid on February 16.
What paper is it?
Is there any No. 2 wheat? I am wondering whether there is any No. 5 in the Manitoba district.

I do not know how western farmers will react to the suggestion the hon. member made with regard to eastern farmers buying directly. They might be pleased with it but it would not suit the hon. member for Assiniboia, of course.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said a lot of things, most of which I will let the minister answer because I think the minister will answer him very effectively. However, there are one or two points I should like to make with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia. He complained about the minister making a comparison of farm incomes when the trend definitely shows an upward movement. Why? He also complained very bitterly about the deficiency payment method used in the marketing of hogs and eggs. He neglected to mention, of course, that not only had the market been stabilized but so had production and that accompanying this stabilization there had been a very welcome increase in the price received by the producer. He forgot very conveniently that there was a surplus of over 1 million pounds of pork which has now been sold because of the action of the government, and I think this answers the hon. member for Assiniboia very effectively.
The hon. member went on to say something about the slow movement of grain from the prairie provinces. However, he conveniently forgot or just neglected to mention a certain strike of grain handlers on the Pacific coast. I want to refer to that strike because in complaining about low farm incomes and farmers being forced to the wall the hon. member neglected to mention the strike.
I shall read a statement from the Western Producer of Thursday, December 8, 1960. This is a paper which is well known by the hon. member and to the policy of which I believe he subscribes.
-in the Western Producer dated the 10th of last month, where it points out that the basic wages

This is higher than the basic wage paid by any other industry in Canada for semi-skilled labour. Yet they have been offered an increase of 5 per cent which will make their basic wage $2.23 an hour. In addition their position lends itself to considerable overtime for which they get time and a half for weekdays or $3.34 per hour and double time or $4.46 per hour for Sundays and statutory holidays.

That is not true. That is a false statement.

I just said, Mr. Chairman, that I thought that, and it appeared to me that way.

Feed mill policy 'legalized robbery'.
The hon. member created quite a little fuss in another part of this house-in one of its committees as a matter of fact-by referring to this "legalized robbery". I think what I have quoted on the record explains this very well.

The western agricultural conference in Saskatoon last week supported new Canadian wheat board regulations permitting farmers to deliver grain to feed mills outside of wheat board price and quota controls.
Of course, my hon. friend from Assiniboia, Mr. Chairman, and his little group, as well as the political party that may result from this dreamed of marriage, have all the answers to all our problems. I will read from a little item in the same Western Producer:
As for the C.C.F. having the answers to our problems, all they could bring us is 100 per cent taxation and we would all end up as employees of the state and all freedom would be lost.
I must agree with that statement.
I do not.

Of course you do not, belonging to that party.

Mr. Chairman, in conclusion I have a couple of recommendations which I should like to make to the minister and the government. I have made these recommendations before during the past two years. I should like to ask the minister and the government to give their serious consideration to the inclusion of forage crop seeds-by this I refer to clovers, alfalfas and leguminous crops-in the provisions of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. My constituency and that of my colleague from Jasper-Edson are very heavy producers of clovers, alfalfas and other leguminous crops. Having has good crops the last few years we find the farmers receiving as low as three and four cents a pound for some of their seed. I think it would be a very great boon to a rather large section of Alberta agriculture, and the Peace river, if these crops were brought under the provisions of this act.
I must, of course, make my perennial plea that the government pay the acreage payments to western producers again in 1961 on the same basis as in 1958 and 1960. I think general satisfaction has been expressed by the constituents I represent in this method of assistance which has done far more than could possibly have been imagined at the time the first payments were made, not only for the general welfare but for the economy as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, as I was saying, if we take into account the national gross income and if we divide it by the present number of farmers, it is obvious that the per capita income has increased. However, I think we should take into account the production cost which has increased substantially.
While those figures on the decrease of farmers in Canada may help the minister in arriving at his income figure, I am sure, on the other hand, that those figures are certainly not to the liking of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) because they are probably included in the number of unemployed we now have in Canada.
I expected the minister to praise the achievements of the government. I expected, for instance, to hear him refer, as several of his colleagues have done in and out of the house, to crop insurance, to the stabilization prices act and to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. We also asked a question about the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and we found out that, probably, that measure has probably not yet been been brought to the attention of all farmers, or at least a great majority of them, since only a few of them took advantage of it.

Reports indicate that the 10-cent reduction in the retail price from the present level of around 69 to 71 cents a pound would not affect the price support of 64 cents. The plan is aimed at reducing Canada's butter surplus by making it more competitive with margarine.

Mr. Chairman, following the inventory made of the quantity of butter now in existence in Canada, we expected the minister to announce that policy. But he did not, probably for the reason mentioned in that article of the Rural Co-operator, because the cabinet has not yet taken any decision.
However, if we look at the statistics on December 1, 1960, we realize that there were 131,684,000 pounds of butter in Canada. It seems it would have been a marvellous opportunity and a good policy to establish at once that butter subsidy, which surely would not have failed to help decrease that inventory and encourage farmers who are dependent mostly on dairy farming.
The same policy, for instance, could have applied to powdered skim milk, with an inventory of 4.3 million pounds. The same goes for canned pork, with an inventory of 35.8 million pounds.
Apart from that policy of subsidies, another course could be followed, similar to the policy which is carried out now in the United States. It would consist in distributing to the unemployed, of whom there are approximately 700,000 in Canada, part of the farm surplus. Such action would certainly relieve their present plight.
Mr. Chairman, I was also somewhat surprised to see the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Argue) being shocked by the words of the hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska (Mr. Boulanger). Hon. members who preceded me, including the minister, scarcely mentioned those problems, and only my colleague from Drummond-Arthabaska dealt with them.

I do not think he would want a policy detrimental to the western farmers. To my mind, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska proved moreover, by quoting the figures of the dominion bureau of

statistics, that the farm income did not increase in 1960, but rather declined. To support that assertion, he quoted, as I said, figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics. Only 12 per cent of the Canadians of voting age still live on farms. But a close study of representation in the House of Commons shows that nearly

60 per cent of its members sit for rural areas. The smashing of Quebec's Union Nationale electoral machine by Jean Lesage, and the Tories' ineffectual political handling of French Canada since the 1958 victory, have convinced Conservative strategists that nothing they can do between now and the next campaign will win back this key province. Mr. Chairman, I will simply tell the minister, if he wants his policy to be popular in Quebec, to suggest-and I hope he will have an opportunity to make some comments during the consideration of his estimates-a solution to the problems faced by our farmers.
I believe we are justified in bringing those problems to the attention of the minister since he himself and his colleagues did not have any qualms about making innumerable promises during the electoral campaign of 1957 and 1958. I would say to his colleagues and more particularly to the minister that this failure of the government to keep their promises will hardly help them politically, and even worse, their attitude causes the worst prejudice not only to farmers in Quebec but to those in Canada generally.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on his appointment to this portfolio and to wish him success in this new undertaking.
I may also say that the farmers in Canada, and in particular the western farmers, have welcomed his appointment and judging from what has been said by them on different occasions, they expect he will do justice to this very important department.
Even when the minister was in charge of another department, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, his contribution to the agricultural economy of this country was known and felt in this house, the cabinet, and above all in Canada as a whole. Anybody having any doubt about this need only look at the records of the house to see the truth of what I have said.
To the previous minister of agriculture, the present Minister of National Defence, I should like to express my regret at his leaving the department. He has done impressive work as minister of agriculture but has been called upon to take charge of another department. We wish him the best of luck and we know that he will also do justice to his new department.
Agriculture is a very important part of our national economy. Some people like to prove statistically that agriculture's No. 1 position has been taken over by other industries in

Canada. This may be true to a certain extent, but nobody can deny the fact that in importance it is and still will be Canada's No. 1 industry for a long time to come. If we look back on our agricultural history we find that western grain has been the life of Canadian commerce ever since our pioneers opened up the west for settlement. The purpose of the Crowsnest pass agreement of 1897 was to make it economically possible for the western farmers to produce grain in quantities large enough for the needs of Canadian commerce, and the government of that day considered the agreement to be a step in the best interest of Canada. What was true then in regard to grain produced in 1897 holds true today in regard to such grains as wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed produced now in the west for commercial purposes. The Canadian economy depends on commerce today just as much as it did then. This nonsense which some people talk about removing the Crowsnest pass agreement on freight charges is nothing less than an attempt to scuttle the whole of western agriculture. Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that no one knows this better than our Prime Minister, who has said on many occasions that the Crowsnest pass agreement is the magna carta of western agriculture.
While I am on this subject of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates I should really say something about the rapeseed freight charges. Rapeseed is the only grain not covered by the Crowsnest pass agreement. However, I shall reserve my comments on the subject until another occasion. Instead, I should like to say something with regard to edible oil.
As far as the tariff on edible oilseed is concerned, this indeed presents a very disturbing situation. The biggest single factor discouraging the use of this oil in Canada is the fact that Canadian crushers are allowed to crush American soyabeans and rapeseed in Canada-products which come in free of tariff-and thereby by-pass the 20 per cent tariff which is now in effect on soyabean oil and rapeseed oil. I ask hon. members to note the situation: There is a 20 per cent tariff imposed on the soyabean oil and rape-seed oil, but no tariff whatsoever on soyabeans and rapeseed. This is what is happening in the crushing industry: the Canadian crusher purchases all the Canadian soyabeans and rapeseed. He does not use any of these beans and seeds to crush into oil for Canadian consumption. He uses these to make up the 25 per cent of Canadian material in the oil and meal that he markets in Great Britain and other favoured treaty countries. The soyabean oil that he sells in Canada is made from American beans and rapeseed. In this way he entirely by-passes the 20 per cent 90205-6-154J

tariff on the oil. In illustration of this point I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that margarine production in Canada in 1959 amounted to 152.5 million pounds. Only one tenth of the margarine made in Canada is made from oil seeds grown in this country. The rest is made from oils which come into Canada from the United States duty free.
However, I am happy to see that the Minister of Finance has announced in his supplementary budget that the tariff board is to be instructed to adjust this discriminatory tariff imposed on these edible oils.
I should like to touch on another subject coming within the scope of the Department of Agriculture, namely the price of farm machinery. As you will recall, Mr. Chairman, in the dying days of our last session this question was placed before the standing committee on agriculture so that an investigation might be made. As a member of this committee, I have been looking forward to the resumption of this inquiry. Hon. members know that one of our great problems in the farm industry at the present time is the high price of farm machinery. These prices are out of all proportion to the prices which the farmer receives for his produce and, what is more, the prices of farm machinery are constantly rising year after year while the prices of farm products remain the same or, in some instances, even go down. Is it the high cost of labour which can be blamed for this increase in the price of farm machinery, or are the high profits of the manufacturer responsible for the continued increase in prices? Alternatively, is management at fault for not making a sincere effort to put out an economic machine and hold down the cost of that machine? As a further alternative, is the high cost to be attributed largely to wasteful and expensive methods of distribution? These are questions to which answers must be provided.
I have given very serious thought to the inquiries which have been made into the price structure of farm machinery and I have followed very closely what has been said in the press and on the radio with regard to this matter. In particular, I am interested in a financial statement published by Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited of Winnipeg, Manitoba. According to this statement, the experience of the C.C.I.L. over the years has been that in relation to total sales of slightly more than $54 million there has been a net saving of $5,640,000. This saving has been made on sales which represent a very small percentage of total machine sales in western Canada. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to speak about wheat, oats, barley, rye, the Canadian wheat board, box car allocations or deficiency payments. I wish merely to ask a number of questions of the minister relative to the agricultural situation in British Columbia and the attitude of the minister toward it.
I regretted very much the attitude displayed by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin when he spoke earlier. He is an hon. member who does not appear able to ask questions or say anything in , this chamber without putting it

on a completely partisan political basis. The hon. gentleman was never more guilty of that than when he spoke earlier this afternoon. I hope I shall not follow that procedure. Surely charge and counter charge will not assist us in a policy discussion on the agricultural estimates. What is required now is not partisan political discussion with accusations, charges and counter charges. What we require is information from the minister and if we wish to go beyond that in participating in the discussion we are free to present constructive proposals.
I shall attempt not to follow the example set by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin who was guilty of political partisanship in his remarks today. It is good to avoid following that example because sometimes we might be prone to answer that kind of attack in like manner. If I were to indulge in that type of thing today I would probably begin by telling the minister that his government is sabotaging the agricultural industry of British Columbia.
Non-partisan, of course.

However, that is not my attitude. I should like the minister to tell us if he has had time since assuming his important office to raise his eyes beyond the western prairie horizon of rye, oats, wheat and barley and look over the mountains into British Columbia? British Columbia is a mountainous province with four ranges running from north to south. Far too many people do not realize that between those ranges we have some of the most productive agricultural land on the North American continent. Admittedly, sir, I speak as a member from the urban area of Vancouver but I know British Columbia and I love it. With all due respect to every other member in this house, I say that in the Fraser valley of British Columbia, from Vancouver to Hope, in the valley areas, in the mountain ranges, from Salmon Arm, Enderby, Armstrong, Vernon, Penticton, Kelowna, to Osoyoos, we have some of the finest, fertile, productive agricultural lands in North America. This has been proven in the production of soft fruits, hard fruits and vegetables. A change has taken place over the past few years. I tried to raise this matter last session but unfortunately did not get very far with it.
I have lived in Vancouver since 1910, when I was only three years of age. I can remember the productivity of the Fraser valley in regard to berries, and particularly strawberries. Our product went around the world in the shape of jellies and jams, but that situation does not obtain today. Production is now purely for the local market. Why is this so? Because no attention has been paid
Supply-Agriculture
to the buying up of our canneries and factories by people below the border and exporting to Canada their products, but selling them under the Canadian brand.
It is only a few years ago that in the area from Lillooet to Osoyoos there were 16 canneries. Last year only four were left. I have been advised of one in that area which is going to close this year and which I maintain holds a world record for the quality of its products, namely vegetables, peas, tomatoes, and so forth. Why is this so? It is because the area from Lillooet to Osoyoos is three weeks behind production in California. By the time the agricultural producers in the areas I have mentioned are set to market their products California is set to market its surpluses, and moves them into British Columbia. Certain action has been taken by governments in the past in regard to the situation, and this is the reason certain of our canning companies in Canada, and particularly in British Columbia, were bought out. The reason is simple. If the small canning companies are not there, then the producers have no market to which to sell.
I raised this matter last year in regard to tomatoes and the then minister of agriculture-I am glad he is in his seat at the moment-answered to the effect that a subsidy would be granted for the crop year but it would then cease. I still have the letter to that effect from the hon. member. Wheat, oats, barley, rapeseed and rye are important in many parts of Canada, but berries and vegetables are very important to our province of British Columbia. To the best of my information the situation in the coming year will be worse than it was a year ago. Judging from the information sent to me by growers, I am of the opinion that they are very disturbed at the situation. I say to the Minister of Agriculture, through you, Mr. Chairman, that, much as we recognize the emphasis and importance that the minister has placed on agriculture in the prairies, we would like him to take a good look at the maintenance of agriculture in British Columbia. We would like to hear whether the Minister of Agriculture has any special plans for the protection of our berries, our soft fruits and our vegetable industries. We would like to know whether a special, study will be made of the situation there on a production, canning and marketing basis.
We may be known as a lumbering and mining province but, if my memory serves me correctly, our third greatest industry has been agriculture. It has been deteriorating. I fear that it has been neglected and is still being neglected by the federal Department of Agriculture. Just because we may be hemmed in by four mountain ranges

Supply-Agriculture
and 3,000 miles from Ottawa we should not be ignored. We are an integral part of Canada. I gather from this morning's newspapers that we are such an important part of Canada that if plans go through at the dominion-provincial conference we are going to lose out because of the wealth of our province.
I hope I have not fallen into the despicable line of thought of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin by asking the minister to raise his eyes above the Rocky mountains and look at agriculture in British Columbia and advise us as to present plans for the protection of agriculture in our province, in the Fraser valley from Lillooet to Osoyoos. I made a mistake. I almost ignored that most marvellous agricultural area, especially in so far as seeds are concerned, namely Grand Forks. Now that the minister has taken over this most responsible office I ask him whether a special study will be made of the potentialities of agriculture in British Columbia and whether protection will be given to that great industry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join in this debate and make a few comments on agriculture as it pertains to the maritime provinces.
First of all, I should like to extend my congratulations to the minister, both on his appointment as Minister of Agriculture and on the enthusiasm he has brought to this department, which enthusiasm was so apparent when he was minister of northern affairs and national resources. I should like to say to him that I was recently in Nova Scotia and in talking with people keenly interested in the agricultural industry in that province I learned that his recent visit to the maritimes was greeted with enthusiasm He has instilled in the people of our area an outlook so far as agriculture is concerned that we like to see them have. Personally I should like to see him come back to visit our people again and I hope he will do so in the very near future.
It has become a regular custom for members of parliament from Nova Scotia to meet with the executive of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture each year when they come to Ottawa to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Members from Nova Scotia have come to look forward to this annual meeting as an opportunity to get views of those engaged in agriculture in our area and as an opportunity to have brought to our attention those matters which are felt to be most pressing by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture.

At this time I should like to bring some of the suggestions brought to our attention to the attention of the minister in order that he may be fully aware of the attitude of the federation with respect to the different aspects of the industry. At our recent meeting a number of matters were discussed. One thing that is of particular importance to me as the member for Cumberland is their views with regard to the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. This act came into operation some ten years or more ago and was put into effect to help marsh owners in our province to improve their lands throught a system of dikes, aboiteaux and dams.
When the act was brought into force some ten years ago it was indicated there would have to be an agreement between the federal and provincial governments and the farm bodies in the different areas in order that all might be aware of the importance of the projects that would be undertaken. At that time an agreeement was made between the federal government and the province that when the work was concluded the province and the marsh owners would take over the maintenance of the projects that had been undertaken. No doubt when this was agreed upon no one imagined the magnitude of the work that would be carried out under the act and in the light of that fact an agreement was reached.
Today, however, as the work draws to a close the province and the marsh bodies both see the tremendous costs that will fall upon them should the maintenance be placed on their shoulders alone. Because of this fact they have emphasized very strongly that the federal government should endeavour to phase in the maintenance work under the agricultural rehabilitation and development legislation. This would mean that those lands that have been greatly improved in value would not now have to be left to revert to their former condition, for if the federal government were to insist that the maintenance be carried out by the province and the marsh bodies that would no doubt be the result over a long period.
It is quite apparent that neither the province nor the marsh bodies can accept the financial obligations that would be placed upon them if the federal government were to insist on their maintaining the work that has been done. If we are to endeavour to keep these lands that have been tremendously improved as the result of the work carried out for the generations of today and tomorrow we must give further assistance and endeavour to phase in this work under the

new rural rehabilitation scheme. I ask the minister to give this matter his most serious consideration.
Another point I should like to bring to the minister's attention in this regard is that the headquarters of the M.M.R.A. administration are at present located in Amherst and over the period of the operation of the act a very large and competent staff has been built up consisting of people who are well aware of the problems of the area and who have created a great deal of good will in their negotiations with the marsh bodies. It is my hope that the department will give consideration to using the facilities and the skills that are readily available at Amherst to carry out the provisions of the agricultural rehabilitation and development legislation.
May I also bring to the minister's attention some other points that were emphasized by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture with regard to which I would appreciate his serious consideration. One point they raised which I have also brought up in debates in the house has to do with unemployment insurance for farm labourers. I know this matter is under study at the present time by the Department of Labour. The representatives of the federation point out that it is a problem that has caused farmers in the maritime provinces a great deal of difficulty in attracting seasonal help. The reason is a simple one. If such people work for someone other than a farmer they are able to get stamps and to qualify for seasonal or regular benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. If they work for farmers they are not able to obtain these benefits which are so very important to many people in the maritime provinces. I realize that the minister is keenly aware of the circumstances of our farmers in this regard.
Another matter for which they request consideration has to do with the establishment of total disability insurance to be incorporated in the terms of loans made through the farm credit corporation. In Nova Scotia our provincial agricultural loans contain a provision guaranteeing this total disability insurance. The Nova Scotia federation have recommended that this be considered by the federal government as well, and incorporated in our farm credit legislation. It is my belief that we recently have made death disability insurance available through this legislation to farmers at their discretion if the loans are not supervised, but it is mandatory if loans are supervised. I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the placing of total disability insurance in this scheme as well.

The Nova Scotia federation requests consideration for an increase in the support price for lambs. The federation states that the support price in the maritimes is below that either in Montreal or Toronto, and they wish consideration given to the support price being increased to bring it in line with the prices now available in those two areas.
Another matter which they wished brought to the attention of the government, but one which I feel should more rightly be placed before industry itself, is the equalization of transportation rates on farm machinery in this country. I believe an example could be made in respect of cars better than farm machinery. We know that a car manufactured in Ontario is more expensive in Nova Scotia than in Ontario, while at the same time we find that European cars come to this country and the price is the same in all parts of this country. I should think, since a large proportion of the cars manufactured in Canada are sold in the two central provinces, this problem of equalization would not be a very difficult one. A small increase in the price of cars in Ontario and Quebec would produce enough funds to provide an equal price level across the country. If the European manufacturers see merit in this scheme, I see no reason why our own manufacturers cannot take the initiative in this matter and let the government stay outside, where it should be in respect of such things.
The only other point that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister at this time is the matter of the government's policy on deficiency payments for hogs. I would point out to the minister that last year the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture supported the government when it put this policy into effect. I might therefore point out that as a result of this policy and the attitude of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture, there has been a very substantial increase in the production of hogs in the maritime provinces. As all hon. members know there has been a substantial increase in the price paid for pork since this policy went into effect and as a result of the guidance provided by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture, our farmers have benefited materially.
I do not think there is anything more that I wish to add at this time. I wish to thank you all for listening to my remarks.
