Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the Canadian index, which I think the public archivist or national librarian will concede is a most important reference tool. I think he will also concede that it is typically Canadian and cannot be sold on any remunerative basis to cover the total expenses.
For the last several years it has been supported substantially by the Canada Council; yet we have been told by the head of the Canada Council, both the late Mr. Claxton and Dr. Trueman, that there is no intention on the part of the Canada Council to make this a continuing thing, that the set-up of the council is not such as to permit a whole block of its funds to be gradually nailed down for recurring expenses. This is a popular form of documentation and indexing, but it is immensely useful and at the same time there is no possibility of the service becoming selfsustaining. It is very much a public service.
What contribution can the national library make to this particular indexing; and, since this is a Canadian indexing service, why should it not be the kind of responsibility that the national library undertakes? In essence Canadiana is performing this function for the more permanent kind of publication and the Canadian index of periodicals is, of course, our means of keeping up to date with what is going on in all the periodical publishing fields in Canada. If the national library were to undertake this kind of chore, which seems to be properly within its function, I suggest that it should expand the index so that it will provide the kind of over-all service in the publications field that is not being provided at the present time by the Canadian library association.
The minister has said that the duties of archivist and national librarian dovetail very naturally. In an administrative sense this seems reasonable. I would assume that Dr. Lamb is primarily an administrator, but the point I was trying to make to the minister was that librarianship has become an extremely specialized field. In the field of documentation there is a complexity and a growing experimentation, I might say, in an effort to keep on top of records, and this is one of the outstanding developments of our times in the academic and research fields.
I suggest that the function of the archivist is much different, because archives by their very nature are confined in the main to records of the past and, in the present day, confined properly to public records of the past. While there are common problems in respect of cataloguing, indexing and control of these things, I suggest that librarianship has become more specialized, and that is why I personally feel that the whole field of librarianship would gain through having as


head of the national library a man who was a librarian and who was at the administrative pinnacle in that particular field.
The last point I wish to touch on in these remarks has to do with the suggestion of the minister that the conception of the national library collection has already been well worked out, and there is to be no overlapping in the field of science with the defence research board library or the national research council library. This is fine in that particular area, but I should like to know what is being done about the collections in other Ottawa offices. One of the problems that drives me up the wall as a user of the library of parliament is that when you go there and want a technical book on a specialized subject the library does not tend to have it. It has what I think is a pitiful collection in the economic field, particularly in connection with our resources in the field of forestry and allied fields. If you will take a ruler I think you will find that the books in the field of forestry cover 48 or 50 inches in the library of parliament. This is all the information that is available when we go looking for something to help us to deal with the problems that arise and try to help these industries.
This is all very well as a criticism of the library of parliament. You can go there and ask for a book in this particular field. They say that the forestry branch has an excellent library in this field and that they will get the material for you. I will concede that it does seem unreasonable to place within the library of parliament a specialized or extended collection on forestry and all these other fields for the use of maybe 265 members of parliament or a fraction thereof when just seven, eight or nine blocks away there is a magnificent, well indexed collection on forestry in a library staffed by people who know its contents intimately.
The very same criticism applies to the national library and its scope. Dotted across Ottawa we have these various government libraries. The economic research branch of the Department of Labour has a fairly extensive collection. In fact its collection in this field is a topnotch one. The Department of National Health and Welfare has a good collection. Fairly strong efforts are being made to keep these collections up to date and on a continuing basis, and to provide current reference service to the administrators. Service is also provided to the general public and members of parliament.
As a consequence of these departmental libraries in Ottawa, the spectrum of knowledge is fairly well covered. I will not say it is completely covered, but there is this coverage. What sort of overlapping are we likely to get in the national library? Is there

a plan to take much of the older material from these collections and put it in the national library? The minister suggested in her reply that the concentration was going to be in the field of social sciences. What does she mean by "social sciences"? Just how embracing is that? For example, is Canadian literary history a phase of social science? What kind of collection of novels is planned for the library? Is the library going to concentrate upon Canadian publications, or is it going to be concerned with the best that has been thought and said in the literary field?
I should like to know whether the national library is going to specialize in the collection of federal and provincial records and publications, or is it going to collect those of the commonwealth or of the world generally? Is it planned to have a supply of the "Congressional Record" on hand? Is the national library going to take over responsibility for the collection of all United Nations publications? I should like to have these questions answered in order to have some idea of the collection that is going to grow in the building we are going to have some day.

In answer to a couple of the comments of the hon. member, I might say that ever since the library came into existence in 1952 it has published the Canadian index of periodicals and documentary films. I think the hon. member regretted that there was no such publication available. It has been published every year.
Not by the national library.

Yes, by the national
library.
The Canadian index of periodicals?
The annual Canadian index of periodicals and documentary films has been published every year by the national library since 1952, when the library first came into existence.
What publication is it that is issued by the Canadian library association and supported by the Canada Council?

The Canadian library
association compiles and puts out monthly mimeographed editions. The national library puts these together into a comprehensive index which is an accumulation of the monthly editions.

While I am concerned with the Canada Council paying a considerable part of the cost for this particular service, my question was directed to why this cost was not taken over completely by the national library. I am sorry I missed recognition of
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration that part so far as the cumulative publication is concerned, but I realize, as I am sure the minister does, that the main cost concerns the actual indexing proportion. The cumulative portion is mainly printing, and the charge is not great. If it is not the case that a very large contribution is being made by the national library, I would like to know how much more it would cost for the national library to take over this complete service.

I cannot make an estimate of the additional cost. This is a matter that can be considered and possibly will have to be considered one of these days, but at the present time the information is not available. This whole problem covers a wide field involving many considerations, and I do not think that in a short space of time I can enumerate them all. If the hon. member would like a report in this regard I would be glad to have one prepared.
I might add also, with reference to his comments regarding the information being scattered around, that it is all catalogued, as he probably knows, in the union catalogue which is the key to all the libraries and the books therein. I was wondering as a result of some of the remarks the hon. member made whether he has ever visited the national library.

Mr. Chairman, the reason I would like to know very definitely the role the national library thinks it should play is that we are going to have the Canada Council before the public accounts committee in a few weeks, and I feel that the Canada Council is trying to keep its recurring expenditures and grants as low as possible. If it is seriously considered that the national library could fill this role, it would then follow that there would be more Canada Council money available for scholarships and other things.

I think the best solution to this problem is for the hon. member to consult the national librarian. I understand he has never done that. If he would make an appointment to call on the national librarian I am sure he would be glad to supply the hon. member with the information that is available, and I am sure this would serve his purposes.

The minister made the point that I had never consulted the national librarian. There are a tremendous number of people whom I think all members of parliament would like to consult, but it is very difficult to get around to them all. I feel that members make an attempt to focus their attention on questions and suggestions in so far as the expenditures are concerned, and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration I suppose primarily we should be interested in cutting them down. I was not trying to suggest, as my earlier comments will show, what in effect might be a cutting down of the whole thing by creating a grand institutional library. I am quite pleased to hear that this is not being conceived. If I can break it down more particularly to Ottawa libraries, I know there is a union catalogue; I also know that libraries are growing all the time, and that union catalogues go out of date. It is a large job keeping them up to date.
The hon. member is quite wrong. This catalogue is kept up to date all the time.

Yes, I know that the catalogue is kept up to date all the time, but I was going on to say that this takes considerable time on the part of the librarians both in regard to storing the books and in having the index prepared. What I am trying to get from the minister, and I would appreciate a statement from her not at this time but in the future perhaps in letter form, is how the libraries in the public service in Ottawa are going to dovetail in with the national library. I am not speaking in terms of a catalogue that will be kept by the national librarian, but in terms of the actual coverage and placing of books. Because we have a national health and welfare library, will everything in that field be primarily the responsibility of that department and not that of the national library except in so far as indexing or cataloguing is concerned? Will this also apply to the Department of Justice library in the supreme court building, which I understand tends to be a growing one? I would like to know what the liaison is in this field which prevents duplication.
The point that intrigues me is that if these departmental libraries build up their collections in a good way, as I assume most of them are doing, they finally will reach the stage of competition with the national library in terms of its collection because, as I suggested earlier, the government of Canada in its libraries is covering almost the whole spectrum of publications except perhaps in the literary or historical field.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That completes the estimates for which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is responsible. We now go to the Department of Agriculture, vote No. 1. This vote will be found on page 4 of the blue book; the details are on page 93.

Administration branch-
1. Departmental administration, including advisory committee on agricultural services, $991,098.

Mr. Chairman, in presenting the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the fiscal year 1961-62 I should like to point out that the summary and the details of services reflect certain organizational changes which have taken place.
During the past year responsibility for the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners was transferred to the Minister of Agriculture. Also during the year the forest biology division of the research branch was transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Forestry. The total to be voted to the Department of Agriculture in these estimates is $122,202,953. This includes the amount required for the board of grain commissioners, which is $6.5 million.
There is, of course, no estimate provision for the Canadian wheat board. However, the amounts shown as authorized by statute include $49 million for payment of carrying costs under the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and $920,000 for the provision of interest free cash advances to western grain producers. These items were previously carried in the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The amount to be voted, plus that authorized by statute, comes to a total of $172,181,953. The corresponding figure for 1960-61, as shown on page 2, is $205.7 million.
This latter includes the figure for the present fiscal year for the board of grain commissioners for carrying costs of wheat reserves and for advance grain payments. It does not include the amount voted in 1960-61 for the forest biology division. The amounts and details shown for 1961-62 and 1960-61 are therefore drawn on a comparable basis and reflect the requirements for and expenditures on the activities now conducted under the Department of Agriculture.
The committee may be interested in a broad break-down of the $122.2 million among the main categories of departmental activities. The amount required for research is $28.8 million, which is 24 per cent of the total. The administration of legislation requires $32.4 million, or 28 per cent of the total. This covers the wide range of legislation administered by the department, including the grading of farm products, animal and plant health, the Canada Grain Act, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act. For rehabilitation, which includes P.F.R.A. in western Canada and

M.M.R.A. in the maritimes, $27.2 million is required. This is 22 per cent of the total. Grants and subsidies require $31.2 million, which is 25 per cent of the total.
The main item in this category is freight assistance on western feed grains, for which $20 million is provided. Included in this category also are quality premium payments on hogs and cheese, lime assistance, grants to fairs and exhibitions and to agricultural organizations. The balance of the vote, some $2.6 million, is required for departmental administration, which includes the economics division.
The committee will note that the amount to be voted in these estimates is $40.5 million less than that granted for the 1960-61 fiscal year. The figure for the present fiscal year, however, includes supplementary estimates to date, the largest item in which was the $42 million for western grain producers' acreage payments. Excluding that amount, these estimates show an increase of $1.5 million over the amount provided for the year ending on March 31.
It will be noted in the details that there are increases in some votes and decreases in others. The largest category of increases is for salaries, which are higher by $7.6 million, due mostly to increases in salary rates. The actual staff increase provided for next year is the equivalent of 73 positions, which is six tenths of 1 per cent of the present staff total. The next largest increase, of almost $2 million, is in the vote for construction of works under land rehabilitation. This is accounted for by greater activity in the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam. In fact $2.6 million more will be required for that project in 1961-62 than was required in 1960-61.
I may say that construction of the dam is proceeding at a satisfactory pace, and on schedule. Stage 1 of the embankment has been completed and stage 2 is nearing completion. Work is proceeding on the downstream diversion tunnels. Contracts will be let shortly for the upstream diversion tunnels and for stage 3 of the embankment.
I think I need not take the time of the committee at this stage to go into details of individual items of expenditure. I know that many hon. members of the committee will be interested enough to discuss these subjects under the respective votes. I do wish to say a word about farm income. In any analysis of farm income in recent years it soon becomes apparent that after the war we were in what can be described as a sellers' market. This was the period of reconstruction in Europe; this was the period of the Korean war. Since about 1953, and possibly starting with the calendar year 1954, we have entered
Supply-Agriculture
into a buyers' market. Our Canadian industry and Canadian farmers are now faced more than ever before with the crash of competition.
I thought the committee might be interested in seeing just how we were making out in increasing farm income in this period of the buyers' market, or this competitive period which we are now in. I have put together some figures obtained from the dominion bureau of statistics. These figures give total cash income, which does include supplementary payments by the federal government.
I am going to read these figures by calendar years. Perhaps some hon. members will wish to copy them down, so I will read them slowly enough for that to be done. In 1954 the total cash income was $2,378 billion; in 1955 it was $2,384 billion; in 1956 it was $2,647 billion; in 1957 it was $2,575 billion. If one adds these figures together and works out the average, the average total cash income for farmers in Canada for those four years, the first four years of the buyers' market, comes to $2,493 billion. The figure for 1958 was $2,873 billion; the figure for 1959 was $2,808 billion; the figure for 1960, which is not yet final from the D.B.S., was $2,861 billion. If you add the last three figures you will find that the average total cash income for each of those years was $2,847 billions.
Therefore the conclusion which can be derived from this analysis is that during each of those three calendar years there was an increase in the total cash income to the farmers of Canada amounting to more than $350 million. I think this does indicate in some measure the efforts of the government not only to stabilize farm income but to increase it.
May I ask a question at this point? Does the minister have any figures or statistics showing the increases in the cost of production over the same period of time?

I will deal with that later on when I deal with net income.
The full picture cannot be appreciated until we examine how many farmers there are. There has been a steady decline in the farm population for many years now, so I will give the figures of the number of farmers and then relate them to income. In 1954, in round figures, there were 594,000 farmers in Canada. In 1955 there were 584,000; in 1956,
575.000	and in 1957, 565,000. If you average the number of farmers in those four calendar years the figure comes to approximately
580.000	during that four-year period of the buyers' market. In 1958 the number of farmers is estimated at 555,000. In 1959 the figure is
546.000	and in 1960, 536,000. If you average the number of farmers during that three-year period the figure is approximately 545,000.

Supply-Agriculture
Now, if one takes the average number of farmers in the first four years of this seven-year period of the buyers' market and divides this income among those farmers, the figure of cash income for the years 1954 to 1959 inclusive is $4,303. If one takes the numbers of farmers for the three-year period 1958 to 1960 inclusive and divides the income for the same period among those farmers, the income per farm comes to $5,214. Therefore, comparing the four-year period 1954-57 with the three-year period 1958-60, there is an increase in cash income amounting to $911 per farmer.
It is obvious that this increase in cash income per farm is due, first of all, to the efforts which we have been making to increase farm income and, second, to the fact that there is a smaller number of farmers. By placing these two sets of figures in juxtaposition one can draw, I think, fairly sound conclusions.
Having put on record those figures which deal with total cash income, I should like now to deal with this question which has puzzled farmers for 25 years, namely why it is that farmers do not receive what they call a fair share of the national income. It is not too easy to find some group in our economy which is comparable with the farmers. The only group I can find which seems to give us some basis of comparison comprises those who are engaged in unincorporated non-farm business. So, from the dominion bureau of statistics labour force survey, I am going to put some figures on the record which I think will show how we are making out in our deliberate policy of seeing what we can do to bring farm income up to a fair share of the national income.
The figures I intend to quote now are net farm returns per farm. In 1954 the figure was $1,792. In 1955 it was $2,376. In 1956 it was $2,836, and in 1957 it was $2,133. Adding and averaging, one gets a figure which shows that during this four-year period of the buyers' market the net income of farmers was $2,284. But one should compare this with the income of non-farm unincorporated business. In 1954 non-farm incorporated business received, on the average, $2,883. In 1955 the figure was $3,162; in 1956, $3,341; in 1957, $3,351. The average for this period received by non-farm unincorporated business was $3,184 as compared with $2,284 by the farmers. Put as a percentage of farm income, and relating this to the net income of the non-farm unincorporated group, the farmers received 71.7 per cent of the income received by a reasonably comparable group.
Looking at the figures for the years 1958 and 1959, net farm income in 1958 was $2,891 and in 1959, $2,643. Naturally, we have no

figures yet for 1960 and we shall not have those figures for some time, but those two years I mentioned give an average of $2,767. Non-farm income has been increasing as well in the last two years. In 1958 it was $3,563 and in 1959 it was $3,619, or an average for those two calendar years of $3,591. Expressing these figures as a percentage of net farm income, as related to non-farm income, the percentage for the last two years is 77 per cent. Therefore during the last two calendar years of the buyers' market as compared with the four previous years of the buyers' market, farm income as a percentage of nonfarm income for a comparable group has risen from 71.7 per cent to 77 per cent.
I have been looking at the figures for the first three quarters of 1960. I suggest that when the figures are finally calculated for the calendar year 1960 they will reflect this same upward trend in percentage. Therefore, even though the gradual gain in farm net income as compared with non-farm net income is obvious, it indicates that at the rate we are going it will take about ten years to bring farm net income up to the same percentage level of non-farm income. I put these figures on the record to make clear just one fact, that I do believe we are closing the gap, and this was our intention.
I think it is necessary for me to point out that when one analyses the farm income of this country product by product and region by region, it soon becomes clear that the most variable area is the prairie province area. It soon becomes clear also that the most variable commodities in rate of return are the grain products of western Canada. Therefore it is clear that any government in charge of the selling of wheat, oats and barley has as a first duty to press forward in every way possible to increase the sales of western grain.
I need not tell a committee composed of hon. members knowledgeable with respect to the relationship of eastern and western agriculture that if western Canadian grain is not sold in export markets, the pressure on farmers in every part of the country grows. Therefore it is in the interests of farmers in every part of Canada to closely examine the efforts of the government in the selling of grain in the export market. I do not intend to make any predictions as to what the final total sales will be during this crop year, but I do intend to say something about the efforts we are making to sell grain. I am of the opinion that a good deal of credit goes to my colleague, the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, for the efforts he made through the wheat board in making direct contact with our main customers and in moving into what I call the new market areas

to establish the preliminary contacts to make known the type of wheat we have and its particular qualities that would be an advantage to those countries if they used it. This means there has to be a concerted sales effort. In addition to the general approach of the salesman, we must have a concentrated attack on all the problems that are associated with the selling of this product.
It has become very obvious, I believe, that if we are to continue to sell our flour and wheat in some areas of the world we are going to have to exert every effort at all levels to establish flour mills in those countries and provide the bakeries and demonstration units that must be associated with them to get the maximum consumption of bread in countries that have not used bread before.
We are in full course on this program. It is not going to be easy, because we have competitors in the sale of grain all around the world who have the same idea. We have individual promoters in various countries that are actively seeking the same type of opportunity as individuals or groups. However, it will be of interest, I know, for the committee to be aware that we are in full course on this policy ourselves.
Another point I should like to mention in this connection is that it is now very obvious that there are other things for which wheat can be utilized besides the traditional product, bread. It is no secret that thousands of years ago wheat and barley were used as a staple diet not in the form of bread. In many countries of the world where the tendency to turn to the use of the new product, bread, is slow, it might be possible for us to sell wheat ready for human consumption closer to the natural form.
I want to close off in the next few minutes after making known to the committee what we are doing with respect to another aspect *of our sales efforts. Starting January 1 we set up under the Canadian wheat board a technical services and market research division, the objectives of which are as follows:
1.	To assess at first hand the raw material requirements of the wheat consuming industries in all the potential and actual wheat importing areas of the world.
2.	Where it appears likely that Canadian wheat or flour may be used to advantage in such markets, to work with the consumer industries to the end that they become aware of the advantages that can accrue from the use of such wheat or flour. In areas where the consuming industries are already adequately aware of the advantages offered by the use of Canadian wheat, to maintain close liaison with industrial and government technical personnel to ensure the maximum dis-
Supply-Agriculture
semination of technical information and know how, concerning Canadian wheat and flour.
3.	To establish and maintain technical liaison in the areas of grain handling, wheat breeding, quality assessment and milling and baking in those countries which export wheat, or which could become exporters of wheat, of a type potentially competitive with any of the various grades of Canadian wheat.
4.	To establish liaison with government officials and scientific personnel in underdeveloped countries which might develop in time a bread eating habit. To offer assistance, in these areas, in the establishment of cereal laboratories and in setting up quality criteria.
5.	To write, edit, translate and publish such bulletins, pamphlets, press releases, etc., as appear useful in support of the objectives listed under item 2.
At the head of this new division we have a topnotch cereal chemist, a young man. We have as his assistant an expert on Canadian milling. Serving under them will be four or five younger men with multilanguage ability who will learn the techniques of Canadian milling and the chemical properties of our grain and will be able to deal directly with these countries in their own language to make our present and potential customers aware of how they can use Canadian wheat to better advantage. I think this is the type of thing a corporation would do in selling its products through familiarizing the consumers with the best uses of the products it has available.
I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman, for allowing me to run over the normal hour of adjournment for a few minutes. If hon. members will bear with me for another few seconds I will conclude these remarks.
I cannot, as Minister of Agriculture, let this occasion pass without expressing to the committee and to the country my deep concern and anxiety over what would happen to our growing wheat export sales if there were a major rail strike at a critical time during the movement of grain to tidewater, particularly on the west coast. The consequences to the western farmer would be nothing short of catastrophic. I appeal to labour and to management to approach their responsibilities in the full realization of the public interest involved.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, following the remarks made before the lunch recess by

Supp ly-A griculture
the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton), when he submitted his department's estimates, I wonder what will be the reaction of the Canadian farmers and, particularly, the farmers of my province.
He quoted figures about the net income of farmers in order to prove that their position in 1960 is better than it was in 1954 or in 1955. But he made no mention of the cost of production index, nor of the spread between production costs and prices of agricultural products; he did not mention farm markets, imports, exports, nor did he refer to the question of butter, hogs and eggs. He did not deal with the Agricultural Stabilization Act, particularly with regard to western grain, in spite of the promises made in 1957 and in 1958.
The minister said that in the main estimates for 1961-1962, certain items had been transferred to the Department of Forestry and so on, and that the estimates of the Department of Agriculture showed an increase of $1.5 million for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1961. The main items he mentioned refer to research, where the increase reaches 24 per cent, to administration, with a 28 per cent increase, and to expenditures resulting from subsidies, which went up by about 25 per cent. He added that the cost of implementing the rehabilitation and irrigation program has increased by 25 per cent.
It all looks very interesting when only increases are mentioned. But he did not deal at length with the decrease in certain items. However, we shall have the opportunity to raise this matter while these estimates are under consideration.
In the field of agriculture, as well as in the fields of trade, finance, taxes, unemployment and several others, the over-all situation is such that the farmers are losing confidence in their government and, what is more serious still, are losing confidence in their profession. Who would not lose confidence after the fabulous promises made in 1957 and in 1958 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his candidates when comparing them to the actual facts?
We recall the promises made during the 1957 campaign by the Prime Minister himself when he said in Toronto:
We shall provide farmers with their fair share of the national income by a price support policy for farm products which will be related to cost prices.
And he added:
(Text):
Parity not charity.

(Translation):
During the 1957 session, which preceded the 1958 election, the government saw fit to introduce a bill aiming at the passage of an act for the stabilization of the price of agricultural commodities.
The preamble of that act was of course very promising; it read as follows:
Whereas it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income:
Therefore, the government-
However, after the 1958 election, we saw the government repudiate its promises. Here is the evidence. When, on February 23, 1960, the Liberals moved a non-confidence motion which was in accordance with the preamble of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, 172 Conservative members voted against the motion. In doing that, they voted against their own legislation, against the principles incorporated in that legislation the object of which was to provide farmers with their fair share of the national income.
There are several signs which show that farm income went down in 1959 and 1960, as compared with 1958, the year we were obtaining the full benefit of the legislation passed by a Liberal government.
Mr. Chairman, I will now give figures which do not tally with the ones presented by the Minister of Agriculture this morning, although they are from the dominion bureau of statistics. I quote:
As a matter of fact, the cash Income from the sale of farm products, including payments made under the different acts providing assistance to western farmers, totalled $2.8 billion in 1958, $2,786 billion in 1959 and $2,783 billion In 1960.
We have therefore a continuing reduction of income, in spite of all the legislation passed since 1957 in an effort to stabilize farm income.
If the supplementary payments that are provided under the legislation passed in favour of the western farmers are substracted, we find that the decrease is in the amount of $160 million.
As a matter of fact the cost to the Canadian taxpayers for meeting the commitments under the farm legislation was $77 million in 1960, $22.1 million in 1959 and $60.1 million in 1958.

Moreover, while the farmers were receiving less for their products, they were not paying less for the commodities and services they bought.
The Minister of Agriculture should have told us what has been the increase in the case of commodities and services bought by the farmers these last years.
If we take a basis of 100 for the period 1935-39, we see that the index of goods and services purchased by the farmers in 1956 was 247.6. It went up gradually and in 1957, it was 255.9, in 1958, 259.9, in 1959, 269.5 and, for the first three quarters of 1960, it was 274.4. That means that since 1956, this index has gone up by 26.8.
Let us take now the index of agricultural products sold on the farm. Using the same basis, we see that in 1956, that index was 234.6. It went up in 1958 and in 1959 but went down again during the first 11 months of 1960 to reach 234.7 or nearly the 1956 level.
Therefore, we see that the cost of goods and services purchased by farmers has gone up while the sales price index of farm products is at the 1956 level.
How many times have we heard that the Conservative government would give the farmers the share of Canada's wealth to the production of which they co-operated?
But what is even more serious is the fact that the government and more particularly the Department of Agriculture has just announced in the farm review for January 1961, that the 1961 income would remain at the 1960 level.
When will this government keep its promises? When will it give parity, not charity? When will it put back in each farmer's pocket the $120 that the Liberal government took from him in taxes each year?
Now, I should like to quote what the Minister of Agriculture stated recently to a group of dairy farmers of Canada at a meeting held in Vancouver.
I want to quote these few words to show how the statements of the Minister of Agriculture in this house can differ from the ones he makes elsewhere.
Here is what he said:
(Text):
The purposes are, first of all to take out the ups and downs and to stabilize prices; the second purpose, in so far as products consumed in Canada are concerned, is to use this as a platform on which we can begin to build up the returns to agriculture so as to give them a fair share of
Supply-Agriculture
the national income or, in other words, moving towards parity of income. This is not charity- this is using the legislative power to give the farmer some of the protection that the other segments of the economy have had. You all know what I am talking about.
The working man has the protection of provincial legislation which sets the minimum wage. He has the protection of the tariff for the goods that he produces for the home market. He has the protection of unions if he works in an organized industry where the union bargains to make sure that he gets his share of the national income. The farmer has not got this kind of help. The businessman also has the protection of a tariff if he is producing for the home market. He has the right to set his own price on the basis of cost, plus a reasonable return. The farmer cannot do that and outside of a few places and commodities where the marketing boards have been used as a bargaining agency the farmers, generally speaking, cannot secure that type of protection.
So what the government has done here is to take advantage of the fact that the federal government is concerned in the future of interprovincial marketing. We have tried to build into the system that act which for the first time is beginning to attack this problem of instability of prices, and to use prices as a device to support and, if possible, raise income.
(Translation):
Since 1957 we have been hearing remarks of that kind from our ministers.
What do they want to say? After the results achieved in farming in the last four years, the remarks of the new Minister of Agriculture today should amount to more than so much hot air. Indeed, the minister should have told the producers to what extent they will have to contribute toward economic activity in the years to come.
Mr. Chairman, I would now like to address myself to the situation of feed grain deliveries in the eastern areas during the summer, until the closing of navigation. We learned in the newspapers that from August to the end of the navigation season, in the harbours of Montreal, Quebec city, Baie Comeau and others, a number of ships were waiting in line for two, three and even four weeks in front of elevators full of grain, particularly wheat for export. Those ships could not unload their cargoes, and there was no feed grain on the eastern markets.
In the meantime, our farmers were having all sorts of difficulties in getting supplies, and when they could get them they had to pay a high premium. Now, this shortage of feed grain on the eastern markets, was due to a decision of the Canadian wheat board to ship only export grades to eastern ports. Incredible losses of the order of $1,000 to $3,000 daily were suffered by ship owners, not to mention the loss suffered by farmers

Supply-A griculture
who saw their operating costs increase on account of the higher prices they had to pay for their feed grain.
Although the oats crop will be considerably increased this year over last year, the Canadian wheat board charged 84J cents a bushel for October oats, compared with 60 cents a bushel paid to western producers, at Fort William.
The feed grain requirements in the eastern areas amount to more than a hundred million bushels a year; and from October to the end of the navigation season, close to 50 million bushels must be shipped to fill the requirements for the winter months. There is not much publicity about this 100 million bushel eastern market, but when a few million bushels are sold abroad, the publicity machine of the Department of Agriculture starts rolling at once. Because of the lack of interest shown by the Canadian wheat board and the government, the eastern farmers will have to pay $300 more per carload for moving their grain than it would have cost them if that grain had been moved by ship at the proper time.
Another consequence the farmers will have to bear will be the one resulting from the discriminatory policy carried out by the board and the government since a decision was made last December 28. May I recall the words used by the Prime Minister himself in a speech made in his home town of Prince Albert, when he said: "From now on, the western mills may also buy their oats, barley and wheat in their own provinces, directly and on the open market, at lower prices than those asked by the board for the domestic market in the east."
Unfortunately for the eastern farmers, he stressed the fact that his government was not taking any position which might be the slightest cause of trouble for the board.
With these words, the Prime Minister gave a blank cheque to the grain mill owners, allowing them to organize for integration. Indeed, with the considerable amounts which they have at their disposal, they will build chicken ranches, pig farms and even packing plants and ultimately take over from the farmers in this country. Then, they will be able to pay their own price for their grain without considering the wheat board or the grain producers.
It is strange that the prairie farmers, who always supported the Canadian wheat board,

should have asked for an authorization to sell their grain without being subjected to the regulations of the board. Since then, they get prices 50 per cent lower than they were getting through the board. Today, they are selling their surplus to the grain mills, to other elevators, to other livestock producers, or else they have to increase the number of their animals to use up their grain.
I should like at this point to deal with two particular areas of the province of Quebec which are affected by feed grain prices, the lake St. John and Chicoutimi areas.
I deplore the fact that the hon. members for those two regions are not in the house to learn of the situation which prevails there.
There are not many Liberal members in the house at this time.
This matter should also be of interest to the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), and yet he is absent.

Mr. Chairman, Canada's subsidy legislation contains rules that are detrimental to certain regions. I will explain how that is so.
To show the difference in transportation costs paid by the farmers who buy grain, I have chosen two points equally distant from Quebec city.
A freight rates analysis shows that the rate between Quebec and Roberval, a distance of 188 miles, is 36 cents. On the other hand, for the same distance, or almost-189 miles -from Quebec to Bic, the rate is 32 cents during summer and 42 cents during winter, or an average of 37 cents.
At this time, the rates between Roberval and Quebec, and Bic and Quebec are identical, to a cent or so, but when we take the grants that are paid towards grain transportation, we notice that the Roberval area receives 43 cents per hundredweight while the Bic people get 67 cents in summer and 68 cents in winter.
Mr. Chairman, that enables us to see the difference between the grain rates in two areas equally distant from Quebec city, and it shows that the lake St. John farmers are at a disadvantage.
Mr. Chairman, I could quote other figures for the towns of Normandin and Mont Joli, which are located respectively at 219 miles and 217 miles from Quebec city, as well as

figures for Chicoutimi and Mont Joli which are located respectively at 228 miles and 217 miles from Quebec city.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the minister should make a survey of the freight rates and tell us in a not too distant future what he intends to do in order to give justice to the lake St. John and Chicoutimi farmers.
In fact, those farmers should be treated on the same basis as those of the rest of the province of Quebec.
The farmers in both these areas have accepted huge sacrifices to remain on the agricultural map of the province of Quebec. They have kept abreast of technological advance, improved their farms, set up cooperatives, and particularly a co-operative packing plant which made it possible to process on the spot meats to be distributed in the area. They have invested millions of dollars, and if their situation does not improve soon, it will become untenable.
It is only with great efforts and sacrifices that those farmers have been able to establish organizations which are the pride of the area.
If they are to preserve the millions of dollars invested in their organizations, it is logical that the government play its part now and treat those farmers in the same way it treats the other farmers in the province.
What I feel can fairly be asked on behalf of the farmers in the province of Quebec is this:
1.	The same grain transportation grants for farmers of Saguenay and lake St. John areas as the grants now being paid to the farmers in the other parts of the province.
I wish to point out that transportation costs have increased from 25 cents per hundred weight in 1939 to 66 cents, while those in western Canada did not increase correspondingly.
I think the responsibility to make up for the C.N.R. deficits does not rest with the farmers of Quebec, and especially not with those in the Saguenay and lake St. John districts.
2.	That the co-operatives, the mills and the farmers should have free access to the feed grain market of western Canada, on the same basis as the western mills. That they should not be compelled to negotiate with the Canadian wheat board.
In the United States, the grain trade is free. The producer may sell to the government or on the market. That is why he can compete with the Canadian market, specially in the poultry field.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the members of the committee for allowing me to complete my remarks, and I can assure you that I shall be rather brief.
If the government does not want to agree to a free market, let there be increased assistance to transport of grain to the east, in order that producers may be on the same footing as those of the prairie provinces.
3.	A representative of the east, qualified to explain and defend the eastern farmers interests, should be appointed to the executive of the Canadian wheat board.
4.	A grain transport co-ordinator should be appointed to look after supplying eastern farmers at the proper time, so as to spare them the extra cost of rail transport during winter.
5.	Demurrage cost on cars which are not unloaded 48 hours after their arrival should be removed, as is the case for cars remaining on the tracks at Fort William.
Since the Conservative government has been in power and prior to the ministerial reshuffle last fall, the fate of agriculture in Canada has been in the hands of a prime minister, of a minister of agriculture and of a minister of trade and commerce, the three of them representing prairie provinces. Their dream, and that of the present Minister of Agriculture, was to make of Canada the paradise of farmers. They have made promises but they have not kept them. If we look at agriculture today we realize that the small farmer did not get the promised parity, but merely charity.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member was attacking the Canadian wheat board I wondered about this one fact. Does the hon. member think that

Supply-Agriculture
the Canadian wheat board has any control over the marketing of oats and barley in eastern Canada?
I know that when farmers in the east want to buy grain they have to go to the wheat board and pay about twice what feed mills are paying right now in the west.

I think the hon. member may have misunderstood my question. I wonder whether I could be permitted to correct the record at this time. The Canadian wheat board has nothing whatever to do with the sale of domestic grains in eastern Canada. This is a function of the private grain trade, which includes the co-ops in Quebec. It is their responsibility to buy oats and put them into terminal elevators to sell to the eastern farmer.
The wheat board has a part in so far as it is the board's grain moving through channels to export, but so far as domestic grains are concerned the wheat board has nothing whatsoever to do with them east of Fort William.
When farmers in the east buy oats, barley or wheat, why do they pay twice what the feed mills in the west are paying right now?
That has nothing to do with the question.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question? He has deplored the lack of a free market for grain. As I followed his remarks, he was speaking in a national sense. I should like to ask him if it is his belief, and the belief of his party, that the Canadian wheat board should be abolished.

Mr. Chairman, I am a little surprised that the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska is not rising quickly to reply to this very important question, since he is of course considered the official spokesman of the Liberal party-
He is No. 2.
-on agricultural questions. My hon. friend, the No. 2 man, is something of an interloper.
The hon. member for Essex East is No. 1.

No, the hon. member who has just spoken is No. 1. It is just that he gets pushed around once in awhile by the soya bean expert, the hon. member for Essex East. I listened with a great deal of interest this morning to the speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture. There is certainly a great difference between the kind of speech made
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle) .1
by the present Minister of Agriculture, and its manner of delivery, as compared with those made by the long term minister of agriculture of the former administration. This morning, the Minister of Agriculture spoke in quiet and deliberate terms. One would almost have thought one was listening to a very elementary lecture on economics as they affect the agricultural situation. The former minister of agriculture, of course, always spoke in a very loud voice, with great energy and with a glass of water in his hand. He fortified himself very frequently with water as he kept making his points.
Which former minister?

I am referring to the minister of agriculture in the former administration. I said "the long term minister in the former administration", and I referred to the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. As for the present Minister of National Defence, I would not wish to go over the experience he had as minister of agriculture, but he was not a water drinker. The present Minister of Agriculture used a great many statistics this morning. The former minister, the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, was a master in the use of statistics and he used a great number of them whenever he spoke. But I think the present minister has put the former minister to shame. I think my friend Jimmie Gardiner would look like a backrow student who had just entered kindergarten compared with a professional like the present Minister of Agriculture as far as the use of statistics is concerned.
One would never think this was a minister speaking for the Conservative party which used to talk in such eloquent terms about parity prices, a fair share of the national income and an improvement of the farmer's position, or that he was the spokesman for a party which used to talk so eloquently on behalf of the small farmer. Now things have changed. What we got from the Minister of Agriculture when he opened these important estimates was not a review of the government's agricultural policy nor a projection of the prospects for agriculture in the years to come but, rather, a discouraging review of very deplorable conditions in this industry. The most significant figures which the minister used, in my opinion, were those which reflected the decline in the number of agricultural operators and they showed how quickly the small farmer is being pushed to the wall under this administration, as he was under the former administration.
I was surprised that the present Minister of Agriculture did not review this thing which they used to call the farmers' charter of rights, known about the country as Bill

237, under which farmers were to get this parity of income and receive by way of deficiency payment technique the kind of support prices for which they have been asking for so many years.
On a point of order, the hon. member for Assiniboia has used two terms-"pushed to the wall" and "parity prices". I should like to have definitions of those two terms.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is not a point of order.
Some members around here learn slowly. The odd one never learns at all.
That's right.

Under this great charter of agricultural rights the farmer has not been faring well, and I think it was significant that the Minister of Agriculture did not refer in his discourse this morning to the effect of the prices stabilization act upon the prices which have been paid to the farmer. I was, of course, for many years a sharp critic of Mr. Gardiner because the average prices established under this legislation were not payable, as some of us felt they should be, directly to the producer, or they were not guaranteed to the producer. Instead, they were paid to the packing companies and the farmer had to deal with the packing companies and do what he could to get from them the established floor. The deficiency payment technique has provided little assistance to agriculture producers because there is no certainty about the way in which the legislation operates. There is no certainty that a farmer who receives less than the stated average national price will recover his losses. As a matter of fact, his chances of recovering those losses are very poor indeed. No deficiency payment has been made in respect of hogs, yet in at least three months, February, March and April, prices less than the stated national average were received by producers who marketed hogs in those months and such people have in fact incurred a very distinct loss which they have no hope of recovering.
This type of so-called support has been used in connection with the marketing of eggs and as in this field I suggest it has been a very dismal failure from the standpoint of the producer. If, as the present Minister of National Defence used to say, one of the purposes of this type of support was to reduce production at times when there appeared to be a surplus, then it has been successful. However, the reduction has been brought about by paying very low prices to 90205-6-153J
Supply-Agriculture
producers and by providing nowhere near the national average price for all the eggs farmers have sold.
I have in my hand a report from the Department of Agriculture showing egg prices paid to producers on a Tuesday of each month at Regina and this shows that in January, 1960, the average price for grade A large eggs was 16 cents. In February, it was 15 cents, in March 26 cents, in April 29 cents, in May 24 cents. These are the lowest prices that have been paid at that point for a great number of years, perhaps since the war years. If one takes these prices for the year and averages them, one finds that the average price for grade A large eggs is approximately 29 cents a dozen. Yet in 1956, the last full year before this government came to power the average price on the same basis was 38 cents a dozen.
Have you got the figures for the balance of the year?

I have to be fair and say there was a deficiency payment made. According to the Canadian federation of agriculture bulletin it works out at 2.4 cents on the average for the year. If one takes that 2.4 cents and adds it to the average I have put on the record today one finds that the producers have lost six cents a dozen or even more under this kind of support policy as compared with the prices they were paid in 1956. The whole point I am making is this. Under the present policy followed by the government there is no floor, no certain assurance-
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member-

I have the floor and I intend to keep it until I have concluded my remarks. The minister may then ask all the questions he likes. I was saying that under this policy there is no certain floor under eggs or hogs. It is the rough average method with the deficiency payment technique which may result in no payment being made even when prices are below the floor or there may be a tiny payment as was the case with regard to eggs. The present government is a Conservative government-
Hear, hear.
Progressive Conservative.

It has its own philosophy. It is a belief in the free market system. The government has followed that belief consistently. It has dumped hogs and eggs on the competitive market without a floor. There is no indication that step by step other products that have been stabilized for a long time

Supply-Agriculture
will not be put on the open market at great expense to the agricultural producer.
I think it was significant that the minister made no reference to butter. According to the hints we receive there will be some changes, and butter will be subjected to the deficiency payment technique. If that technique is applied to butter, I hope it will be used only in conjunction with a floor price and not as an average price so that the producers of butter may have a certain guarantee instead of this nebulous, will o' the wisp assurance that is contained in the so-called prices stabilization legislation.
I offer no objection to this as a policy so long as the government does not lower the return to the producers by putting butter in the same category as eggs and hogs, thus helping to bring about the ruination of the butter producer.
There have been some agreeable indications in recent days of additional sales of wheat being made to certain countries of the world. These are welcome and I hope these additions to our regular markets may be maintained.
I believe the minister will agree that some of these sales, and particularly the sale to China, was in the nature of a windfall or extraordinary sale. China faces a famine situation and is unable to buy from the United States the grain she requires. Because of the famine condition and the attitude of the United States with respect to the sale of commodities to that country, Canada was successful in making sales in that market. I am pleased about those sales, but a great deal more must be done to bring about increased grain sales if we are to have any hope of adequate sales on a longer term basis. What has been going on is not so good as to give the government great cause for joy. I have in my hand the last published statistical summary of the board of grain commissioners, dated February 15. It shows overseas clearances of wheat this year to date to be 141 million bushels as compared with 138 million bushels last year, a moderate improvement. Examining other sales, we find that the sale of barley has dropped by an amount greater than the increase in wheat sales. Barley exports have been reduced from 20.6 million bushels to 6.2 million bushels.
What is our surplus of barley?

If one takes the overseas clearances for all grains to date this year one finds they have been 157.3 million bushels as compared with 167.6 million bushels last year, a total aggregate drop of 10 million bushels.

The minister said the situation was not satisfactory. This year it is even less satisfactory than last year in terms of our accomplishments to this point.
It has been said, and I think accurately, that grain is sold through what might be called a pipe line and that in order that a producer at the extreme end of the pipe line may feed his grain through, the grain obviously must come out at the other end. There is a very accurate relationship over a period of time between farmers' marketings and sales of Canadian grain.
Farmers' marketings are reflected with some variations in the quotas that prevail. The quotas prevailing in western Canada today leave much to be desired.

Thanks to the grain
handlers' strike.

The grain handlers' strike had precious little to do with the worst set of statistics relating to Manitoba. After all, Manitoba is on the eastern side. I received a bulletin on February 22 indicating that as of February 8, 160 points in Manitoba were still on a 1-bushel quota as compared with 121 points last year at the same time. There were 153 points on a 2-bushel quota compared with 116 points last year. Last year the number of points on 3-bushel quotas and 4-bushel quotas were much higher than they are this year.
Saskatchewan, as of this date, still has 99 points on a 1-bushel quota and 661 points on a 2-bushel quota. Alberta, where one would have expected this great disaster to have had the worst possible effect, is at the moment in a better position than Saskatchewan or Manitoba in that only 6 points are on a 1-bushel quota; 168 points are on a 2-bushel quota, and 373 points are on a 3-bushel quota.
I plead with the minister to exercise every effort before the end of the crop year to equalize the quotas for grain. The minister knows as well as I do, and perhaps even better, that his area has suffered in the past with respect to delivery quotas. His constituency and mine are on the apex of deliveries, as it were. In some years we cannot take advantage of the eastern deliveries and in others we cannot take advantage of the western deliveries; we have to wait to the last. This has been difficult for producers in our part of western Canada.
The farmers' union has put forward a substantial point deserving of consideration by the minister. They ask that there be a guaranteed quota delivery. The guarantee should be such that if the wheat board is unable to take delivery by the end of the crop year then the difference could be paid

to the producer for the grain on his farm. If an 8-bushel quota were guaranteed, as was requested, and a farmer at a given point could market only a 6-bushel quota the board should be prepared to buy the difference on the farm in the farmer's storage. The board could then take its own good time in moving out the grain in the days ahead. By this method some equality would be established in the marketing of grain. I suggest that equality is needed and is long overdue.

Did we not
equalize the quotas last year?
They were not too bad last year. The marketings were not equalized but less damage was done last year by this method than on former occasions, and I was very pleased to see some improvement.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Improvement under a Conservative government.

The hottest issue at the moment, as far as the Department of Agriculture is concerned, is this whole question of the government having allowed the feed mills in western Canada legally to buy grain at bankrupt prices and to go into a system of stealing, in a legal way, a substantial part of the farmer's normal returns from grain. I feel that this action has amounted to an abdication of principle. It has been a great mistake. Ninety eight per cent of the farmers will lose the chance to deliver this amount of grain through a quota system. The fact that 98 per cent of the farmers will not be marketing grain to the feed mills means that greater pressure will be placed upon them to go into the livestock business to an increasing extent. This means-and there is no argument about this-that the total income of western producers from grain will be lost because the prices paid by the feed mills in western Canada today are lower than the wheat board prices, and in some instances the final prices are disgracefully low.
The minister has promised to take a look at this. I hope he will take a thorough look at it, and I express the strong hope that this mistake will be corrected in the next marketing year. After all, the excuse for doing this has been that the wheat board could not police its quotas. The actions of the wheat board were upheld by the courts. The Supreme Court of Canada said that the wheat board had the right to police its quota for all mills, agreement, mills and non-agreement mills. Once the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the wheat board this government in effect repudiated the decision of the courts by saying, we are changing the rules and the feed mills will be allowed "legally" to get this grain at bootleg prices.
Supply-Agriculture
Undoubtedly, this has been a severe blow to the system of orderly marketing of grain. What happened in the committee this afternoon spelled out exactly what I feared would happen. In the committee this afternoon no less a person that the official agricultural spokesman for the official opposition said it was his opinion that the grain going to feed mills in eastern Canada should be removed from wheat board control. The pressure that goes with this position taken by the official opposition, together with the natural desire of people in eastern Canada to get their grain at the lowest possible price, suggests that those of us who said this was the thin edge of the wedge that would lead to greater pressure being placed on the government to open the door much wider have been proven correct.
I am disappointed with the stand taken by the Liberal party. I think the official stand they have taken today has been a great mistake. They had better have a caucus and take another look at this subject because the people whom I represent will not be happy to learn that the position of the Liberal party opens the door-
May I ask the hon. member a question?

When I finish the hon. member may ask all the questions he likes.
I appreciate the reasons given for this action, but I think the sooner we return to the position of ensuring that the wheat board quota regulations shall be enforced on all mills in all parts of Canada the better it will be for the Canadian producer and for everyone concerned in this field.
I had hoped the government would tell us today what they were going to do to improve the income position of the farmer. I was curious to learn from the minister whether it was the intention of the government once again to pay the $1 an acre to farmers in the west, amounting to $40 million or $42 million. I would be interested in knowing whether the government intends to change the method by which this payment is made, if it is going to be made, and put it on the unit system, but there was no comment on that.
The Minister of Agriculture wound up his remarks by giving it as his opinion that a railway strike would place the agricultural producers of Canada in a very difficult position. He called on railway and management to do everything possible to avert a strike. I agree with the minister's statements. I suggest that one of the main reasons we are in this position today is the failure of the government to do anything last fall, except procrastinate and postpone the trouble. They

supply-Agriculture
said, "We will not settle it in December; we will postpone it until May 16 and then we shall have to settle it all over again," or the railways can go to the board of transport commissioners and get another hike in freight rates which are already too high.
I think the minister might have singled out management a little more in his remarks. The railway workers said, "We will accept the conciliation board report". I cannot speak for them, but I would not be at all surprised if they would accept the report today if the management of the railway companies were prepared to do the same. The minister lumps them together, although it was the railway companies which refused to settle on the basis of the conciliation board report.
Do you always support that policy?

The government has a great responsibility to deal with the agricultural situation. I suggest that to do that these steps should be taken.
First, the government should exert every effort to move the surplus of grain within this country to the markets of the world and to the people who need it.
Second, the government, instead of weakening the orderly system of marketing, should maintain it and expand it.
Third, the government should give every help and assistance to the development of the co-operative movement in Canada at the producer and consumer level, a movement that I think can be of great service to the agricultural producers. To this end I would suggest that, at least for a beginning a co-operative branch should be set up in the Department of Agriculture to lend encouragement to the co-operatives in Canada.
Fourth, I suggest that it is time the government defined its income supports for agricultural producers and spelled out just how and what it is going to do to fulfil its commitments to Canadian producers that would provide them with a fair share of the national income.

Will the hon. member permit a question? I did not have much luck with my questions to the official agricultural spokesman for the Liberal party. Perhaps the last speaker knows a little bit more about agriculture. He has deplored the falling grain markets in western Canada. Unfortunately for him he mentioned barley. I should like to ask the hon. member if he recalls that the province of Alberta, and Saskatchewan to some degree, lost a market for pearling barley in the Orient by virtue of a strike of longshoremen on the Pacific coast which was fully supported and ardently advocated by his party.
Mr. Chairman, that statement is another lie. It is a real lie.
Oh, oh.

I do not accuse the hon. member of having lied but it is a lie to say that this political party supported that strike. We had nothing to do with the strike in any way, shape or form. As a political movement we offered no support on this issue in any way, shape or form.
You endorsed it.

That is not true either. That is another statement that is completely false. What I suggested was that the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Labour and the government, who have jurisdiction over such works as terminal elevators which have been declared works for the general advantage of Canada, should have done more than sit in their seats and say it was up to somebody else to do something instead of proceeding as they should have to Vancouver and trying to do something to bring the parties together.

Mr. Chairman, my first remarks must be, of course, to express my satisfaction and that of the people I represent with the upward trend in both gross and net farm income. The people in the area I represent are quite pleased with the trend and I think they will continue to be pleased. Like the minister, I sincerely hope for a stay in the trend of farm population away from the farms, and I think the efforts of the government are wholly bent in that direction.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska has referred to some promises made with regard to farmers and farm incomes and so on in the campaigns in 1957 and 1958. I should like to refer to some more recent promises made not by members of the government but made at the so-called great national Liberal rally. I should like to refer to the Country Guide for February, 1961. In that issue there is an article with a headline in red, naturally, reading, "Buying the Vote". The article reads in part as follows:
The Liberal rally held in Ottawa early last month may have made the party faithful who were present glow with enthusiasm, but on at least two counts it was a sad performance .. .
From an agricultural standpoint, the Liberal rally seemed to be completely bewildered and without inspiration. Promising western grain growers a parity price on their first 300 bushels of deliveries each year is not an answer to the grain problem.

The article goes on to say:

He will find that we do not have a surplus of feed grain but we do have a rather large surplus of wheat.
With reference to the stand of the official opposition with respect to agriculture, I go back to something which was said by "farmer Paul" as he was referred to in the Ottawa Journal last fall. The article in the Journal reads in part as follows:
Mr. Martin, beaming at the government benches as he concluded a speech, said that he might have made mistakes here and there. "I will pit my zeal and my desire"-
He said it smilingly, of course.

"to do something to assist the western farmer against what my hon. friend promised and has failed to do."
I do not look upon the efforts in recent weeks as evidence of failure when we sell over 50 million bushels of grain. In "Ottawa Report" of February 14, 1961, prepared for the Thompson publications, the hon. member for Essex East is also referred to as the "wicked fairy and his mother goose tales". I think the description is very apt.
1 was rather amazed to hear the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska speak about direct half-price sales of grain without quotas to the feed mills. I wondered whether he got his figures from the hon. member for Assiniboia or from the Martin bureau of statistics.
Don't blame me for his figures.
In this regard I should like to refer to certain information which appeared in a newspaper recently. The prices are given that were being paid on February 16.
What paper is it?
Is there any No. 2 wheat? I am wondering whether there is any No. 5 in the Manitoba district.

I do not know how western farmers will react to the suggestion the hon. member made with regard to eastern farmers buying directly. They might be pleased with it but it would not suit the hon. member for Assiniboia, of course.
The hon. member for Assiniboia said a lot of things, most of which I will let the minister answer because I think the minister will answer him very effectively. He complained about the minister making a comparison of farm incomes when the trend definitely shows an upward movement. Why? He also complained very bitterly about the deficiency payment method used in the marketing of hogs and eggs. He neglected to mention, of course, that not only had the market been stabilized but so had production and that accompanying this stabilization there had been a very welcome increase in the price received by the producer. Of course, my hon. friend from Assiniboia, Mr. Chairman, and his little group, as well as the political party that may result from this dreamed of marriage, have all the answers to all our problems. I will read from a little item in the same Western Producer:

Mr. Chairman, in conclusion I have a couple of recommendations which I should like to make to the minister and the government. I have made these recommendations before during the past two years. I should like to ask the minister and the government to give their serious consideration to the inclusion of forage crop seeds-by this I refer to clovers, alfalfas and leguminous crops-in the provisions of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. My constituency and that of my colleague from Jasper-Edson are very heavy producers of clovers, alfalfas and other leguminous crops. Having has good crops the last few years we find the farmers receiving as low as three and four cents a pound for some of their seed. I think it would be a very great boon to a rather large section of Alberta agriculture, and the Peace river, if these crops were brought under the provisions of this act.
I must, of course, make my perennial plea that the government pay the acreage payments to western producers again in 1961 on the same basis as in 1958 and 1960. I think general satisfaction has been expressed by the constituents I represent in this method of assistance which has done far more than could possibly have been imagined at the time the first payments were made, not only for the general welfare but for the economy as a whole.
