Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on his appointment to this portfolio and to wish him success in this new undertaking.
I may also say that the farmers in Canada, and in particular the western farmers, have welcomed his appointment and judging from what has been said by them on different occasions, they expect he will do justice to this very important department.
Even when the minister was in charge of another department, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, his contribution to the agricultural economy of this country was known and felt in this house, the cabinet, and above all in Canada as a whole. Anybody having any doubt about this need only look at the records of the house to see the truth of what I have said.
To the previous minister of agriculture, the present Minister of National Defence, I should like to express my regret at his leaving the department. He has done impressive work as minister of agriculture but has been called upon to take charge of another department. We wish him the best of luck and we know that he will also do justice to his new department.
Agriculture is a very important part of our national economy. Some people like to prove statistically that agriculture's No. 1 position has been taken over by other industries in

Canada. This may be true to a certain extent, but nobody can deny the fact that in importance it is and still will be Canada's No. 1 industry for a long time to come. If we look back on our agricultural history we find that western grain has been the life of Canadian commerce ever since our pioneers opened up the west for settlement. The purpose of the Crowsnest pass agreement of 1897 was to make it economically possible for the western farmers to produce grain in quantities large enough for the needs of Canadian commerce, and the government of that day considered the agreement to be a step in the best interest of Canada. What was true then in regard to grain produced in 1897 holds true today in regard to such grains as wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed produced now in the west for commercial purposes. The Canadian economy depends on commerce today just as much as it did then. This nonsense which some people talk about removing the Crowsnest pass agreement on freight charges is nothing less than an attempt to scuttle the whole of western agriculture. Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that no one knows this better than our Prime Minister, who has said on many occasions that the Crowsnest pass agreement is the magna carta of western agriculture.
While I am on this subject of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates I should really say something about the rapeseed freight charges. Rapeseed is the only grain not covered by the Crowsnest pass agreement. However, I shall reserve my comments on the subject until another occasion. Instead, I should like to say something with regard to edible oil.
As far as the tariff on edible oilseed is concerned, this indeed presents a very disturbing situation. The biggest single factor discouraging the use of this oil in Canada is the fact that Canadian crushers are allowed to crush American soyabeans and rapeseed in Canada-products which come in free of tariff-and thereby by-pass the 20 per cent tariff which is now in effect on soyabean oil and rapeseed oil. I ask hon. members to note the situation: There is a 20 per cent tariff imposed on the soyabean oil and rape-seed oil, but no tariff whatsoever on soyabeans and rapeseed. This is what is happening in the crushing industry: the Canadian crusher purchases all the Canadian soyabeans and rapeseed. He does not use any of these beans and seeds to crush into oil for Canadian consumption. He uses these to make up the 25 per cent of Canadian material in the oil and meal that he markets in Great Britain and other favoured treaty countries. The soyabean oil that he sells in Canada is made from American beans and rapeseed. In this way he entirely by-passes the 20 per cent 90205-6-154J

tariff on the oil. In illustration of this point I should like to bring to the attention of hon. members the fact that margarine production in Canada in 1959 amounted to 152.5 million pounds. Only one tenth of the margarine made in Canada is made from oil seeds grown in this country. The rest is made from oils which come into Canada from the United States duty free.
However, I am happy to see that the Minister of Finance has announced in his supplementary budget that the tariff board is to be instructed to adjust this discriminatory tariff imposed on these edible oils.
I should like to touch on another subject coming within the scope of the Department of Agriculture, namely the price of farm machinery. As you will recall, Mr. Chairman, in the dying days of our last session this question was placed before the standing committee on agriculture so that an investigation might be made. As a member of this committee, I have been looking forward to the resumption of this inquiry. Hon. members know that one of our great problems in the farm industry at the present time is the high price of farm machinery. These prices are out of all proportion to the prices which the farmer receives for his produce and, what is more, the prices of farm machinery are constantly rising year after year while the prices of farm products remain the same or, in some instances, even go down. Is it the high cost of labour which can be blamed for this increase in the price of farm machinery, or are the high profits of the manufacturer responsible for the continued increase in prices? Alternatively, is management at fault for not making a sincere effort to put out an economic machine and hold down the cost of that machine? As a further alternative, is the high cost to be attributed largely to wasteful and expensive methods of distribution? These are questions to which answers must be provided.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to speak about wheat, oats, barley, rye, the Canadian wheat board, box car allocations or deficiency payments. I wish merely to ask a number of questions of the minister relative to the agricultural situation in British Columbia and the attitude of the minister toward it.
I regretted very much the attitude displayed by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin when he spoke earlier. He is an hon. member who does not appear able to ask questions or say anything in , this chamber without putting it

on a completely partisan political basis. The hon. gentleman was never more guilty of that than when he spoke earlier this afternoon. I hope I shall not follow that procedure. Surely charge and counter charge will not assist us in a policy discussion on the agricultural estimates. What is required now is not partisan political discussion with accusations, charges and counter charges. What we require is information from the minister and if we wish to go beyond that in participating in the discussion we are free to present constructive proposals.
I shall attempt not to follow the example set by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin who was guilty of political partisanship in his remarks today. It is good to avoid following that example because sometimes we might be prone to answer that kind of attack in like manner. If I were to indulge in that type of thing today I would probably begin by telling the minister that his government is sabotaging the agricultural industry of British Columbia.
Non-partisan, of course.

However, that is not my attitude. I should like the minister to tell us if he has had time since assuming his important office to raise his eyes beyond the western prairie horizon of rye, oats, wheat and barley and look over the mountains into British Columbia? British Columbia is a mountainous province with four ranges running from north to south. Far too many people do not realize that between those ranges we have some of the most productive agricultural land on the North American continent. Admittedly, sir, I speak as a member from the urban area of Vancouver but I know British Columbia and I love it. With all due respect to every other member in this house, I say that in the Fraser valley of British Columbia, from Vancouver to Hope, in the valley areas, in the mountain ranges, from Salmon Arm, Enderby, Armstrong, Vernon, Penticton, Kelowna, to Osoyoos, we have some of the finest, fertile, productive agricultural lands in North America. This has been proven in the production of soft fruits, hard fruits and vegetables. A change has taken place over the past few years. I tried to raise this matter last session but unfortunately did not get very far with it.
I have lived in Vancouver since 1910, when I was only three years of age. I can remember the productivity of the Fraser valley in regard to berries, and particularly strawberries. Our product went around the world in the shape of jellies and jams, but that situation does not obtain today. Production is now purely for the local market. Why is this so? Because no attention has been paid
Supply-Agriculture
to the buying up of our canneries and factories by people below the border and exporting to Canada their products, but selling them under the Canadian brand.
It is only a few years ago that in the area from Lillooet to Osoyoos there were 16 canneries. Last year only four were left. I have been advised of one in that area which is going to close this year and which I maintain holds a world record for the quality of its products, namely vegetables, peas, tomatoes, and so forth. Why is this so? It is because the area from Lillooet to Osoyoos is three weeks behind production in California. By the time the agricultural producers in the areas I have mentioned are set to market their products California is set to market its surpluses, and moves them into British Columbia. Certain action has been taken by governments in the past in regard to the situation, and this is the reason certain of our canning companies in Canada, and particularly in British Columbia, were bought out. The reason is simple. If the small canning companies are not there, then the producers have no market to which to sell.
I raised this matter last year in regard to tomatoes and the then minister of agriculture-I am glad he is in his seat at the moment-answered to the effect that a subsidy would be granted for the crop year but it would then cease. I still have the letter to that effect from the hon. member. Wheat, oats, barley, rapeseed and rye are important in many parts of Canada, but berries and vegetables are very important to our province of British Columbia. To the best of my information the situation in the coming year will be worse than it was a year ago. Judging from the information sent to me by growers, I am of the opinion that they are very disturbed at the situation. I say to the Minister of Agriculture, through you, Mr. Chairman, that, much as we recognize the emphasis and importance that the minister has placed on agriculture in the prairies, we would like him to take a good look at the maintenance of agriculture in British Columbia. We would like to hear whether the Minister of Agriculture has any special plans for the protection of our berries, our soft fruits and our vegetable industries. We would like to know whether a special, study will be made of the situation there on a production, canning and marketing basis.
We may be known as a lumbering and mining province but, if my memory serves me correctly, our third greatest industry has been agriculture. It has been deteriorating. I fear that it has been neglected and is still being neglected by the federal Department of Agriculture. Just because we may be hemmed in by four mountain ranges

and 3,000 miles from Ottawa we should not be ignored. We are an integral part of Canada. I gather from this morning's newspapers that we are such an important part of Canada that if plans go through at the dominion-provincial conference we are going to lose out because of the wealth of our province.
I hope I have not fallen into the despicable line of thought of the hon. member for Wetaskiwin by asking the minister to raise his eyes above the Rocky mountains and look at agriculture in British Columbia and advise us as to present plans for the protection of agriculture in our province, in the Fraser valley from Lillooet to Osoyoos. I made a mistake. I almost ignored that most marvellous agricultural area, especially in so far as seeds are concerned, namely Grand Forks. Now that the minister has taken over this most responsible office I ask him whether a special study will be made of the potentialities of agriculture in British Columbia and whether protection will be given to that great industry?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join in this debate and make a few comments on agriculture as it pertains to the maritime provinces.
First of all, I should like to extend my congratulations to the minister, both on his appointment as Minister of Agriculture and on the enthusiasm he has brought to this department, which enthusiasm was so apparent when he was minister of northern affairs and national resources. I should like to say to him that I was recently in Nova Scotia and in talking with people keenly interested in the agricultural industry in that province I learned that his recent visit to the maritimes was greeted with enthusiasm He has instilled in the people of our area an outlook so far as agriculture is concerned that we like to see them have. Personally I should like to see him come back to visit our people again and I hope he will do so in the very near future.
It has become a regular custom for members of parliament from Nova Scotia to meet with the executive of the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture each year when they come to Ottawa to attend the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Members from Nova Scotia have come to look forward to this annual meeting as an opportunity to get views of those engaged in agriculture in our area and as an opportunity to have brought to our attention those matters which are felt to be most pressing by the Nova Scotia federation of agriculture.

At this time I should like to bring some of the suggestions brought to our attention to the attention of the minister in order that he may be fully aware of the attitude of the federation with respect to the different aspects of the industry. At our recent meeting a number of matters were discussed. One thing that is of particular importance to me as the member for Cumberland is their views with regard to the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act. This act came into operation some ten years or more ago and was put into effect to help marsh owners in our province to improve their lands throught a system of dikes, aboiteaux and dams.
When the act was brought into force some ten years ago it was indicated there would have to be an agreement between the federal and provincial governments and the farm bodies in the different areas in order that all might be aware of the importance of the projects that would be undertaken. At that time an agreeement was made between the federal government and the province that when the work was concluded the province and the marsh owners would take over the maintenance of the projects that had been undertaken. No doubt when this was agreed upon no one imagined the magnitude of the work that would be carried out under the act and in the light of that fact an agreement was reached.
Today, however, as the work draws to a close the province and the marsh bodies both see the tremendous costs that will fall upon them should the maintenance be placed on their shoulders alone. Because of this fact they have emphasized very strongly that the federal government should endeavour to phase in the maintenance work under the agricultural rehabilitation and development legislation. This would mean that those lands that have been greatly improved in value would not now have to be left to revert to their former condition, for if the federal government were to insist that the maintenance be carried out by the province and the marsh bodies that would no doubt be the result over a long period.
It is quite apparent that neither the province nor the marsh bodies can accept the financial obligations that would be placed upon them if the federal government were to insist on their maintaining the work that has been done. If we are to endeavour to keep these lands that have been tremendously improved as the result of the work carried out for the generations of today and tomorrow we must give further assistance and endeavour to phase in this work under the

new rural rehabilitation scheme. I ask the minister to give this matter his most serious consideration.
Another point I should like to bring to the minister's attention in this regard is that the headquarters of the M.M.R.A. administration are at present located in Amherst and over the period of the operation of the act a very large and competent staff has been built up consisting of people who are well aware of the problems of the area and who have created a great deal of good will in their negotiations with the marsh bodies. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-10 to amend the Criminal Code (corporal punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, before referring to the debate which took place on this subject in April of 1959, I should like to outline the approach that I wish to take in the discussion of this bill today. I should like to say something first of all about the present position of judicial corporal punishment in Canada, and say something about the report and recommendations of the House of Commons and Senate committee on capital and corporal punishment of 1956. I want also to review the latest material that has come to the attention of the public on this question, namely the report of the advisory council on treatment of offenders in the United Kingdom presented to the home secretary in November of 1960.
The present situation in Canada is that courts are sentencing people to be lashed and strapped for a series of serious and unpleasant offences. In 1956 seven people were sentenced to the lash and six to the strap; in
1957, 12 to the lash and 21 to the strap; in
1958, 12 to the lash and 8 to the strap. The latest figures that I could obtain from the department indicate that the applications of the lash in 1959 were up above the 1958 figure of 12, and that the strapping figure was down from the 1958 figure of eight. The lash in particular has been applied. Persons have been sentenced to be lashed, and these sentences carried out, for such crimes as incest, assaults on females, indecent assaults on females, rape, sexual intercourse or attempted sexual intercourse, robbery and robbery while armed.
These are not pleasant matters to contemplate by any means, but these are the facts that are before us as members of parliament and we must deal with them. Committees have dealt with them in the past and the recent committee in England which I mentioned has also dealt with them.
A committee of the house and the Senate, as has been recorded in previous debates, recommended after an exhaustive inquiry into
[The Deputy Chairman.]
this subject that corporal punishment should be abolished for any of the offences for which it is prescribed in the Criminal Code. When six o'clock was called on a similar occasion in 1959 and the debate adjourned, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith), who was the final speaker and the only speaker who took a view in opposition to my own on the matter, had a number of things to say about it. I should like to challenge some of them and set the record straight. One of the things he said was this:
I recognize that a great body of public opinion is in favour of the intention behind this bill.
Nothing could be further from the truth. The great body of public opinion in this country is no different in substance than the body of opinion in the United Kingdom or, as I will point out later, the Gallup polls taken in 1960 in the United Kingdom. These Gallup polls indicated that approximately 74 per cent of the people of England favoured the retention of corporal punishment and an indeterminate percentage of those favoured expanding it to other categories of crime. Therefore on that account to begin with I think the hon. member misjudged the situation in Canada.
He went on to say in his remarks:
We have listened this afternoon to a great deal of maudlin sentimentality.
I should like very definitely to set the record straight as far as that particular aspect of this question is concerned. I am not motivated in any sense by a feeling of maudlin sentimentality on the question of corporal punishment. I am concerned primarily with discharging my duty as a member of parliament, to examine the facts and information available on subjects which come before us, reaching a conclusion and casting a vote or taking action to translate that conclusion into the law of the land.
It is in essence a matter of national selfrespect, as far as corporal punishment is concerned. Through the centuries and down through the years we have tried a very fascinating and dazzling variety of brutal methods of punishment. In the main they have failed miserably to accomplish our purpose, which is of course to reduce crime rates and to deal with prisoners after crimes have been committed. At the present time Canada has the great good fortune to have a Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) whose activities in the field of penal reform in my view, and certainly this is a view shared by many people in this country, represent the first important steps forward in 25 years in Canada.
Mr. Walter Stewart of the Toronto Telegram used this caption on an article when

writing in that newspaper yesterday, "Canada's prisons feel the winds of change". These winds of change, this changing attitude on the part of the penal authorities of this country is greatly to be commended. The fact of the matter is, as I said earlier, that the brutal method has in the main failed.
The advisory council on the treatment of offenders, which presented its report to the home secretary of England last November, was composed of a group drawn from men dealing with prisoners and offenders of all kinds. I should like to quote from the statement made on introducing the criminal justice bill in the English house on November 17, by Mr. R. A. Butler, the secretary of state for the home department. He said:
One of these is a V.C., who can hardly have been chosen by reason of being a "softie", and another was the chief officer of the City of London police. I mention this because I think that hon. members may want to know what the constitution of the council is. Its members include many from the professions and walks of life concerned with the prevention of crime and reform of offenders.
So this group of people, at the request of the home secretary, proceeded to examine in exhaustive detail the question of corporal punishment. The situation in England was that judicial corporal punishment had been applied for a wide variety of offences up to the time of the so-called Cadogan committee which was appointed in May of 1937.
Finally in 1948, following the failure of the bill based on that committee's recommendations, which recommendations were to abolish judicial corporal punishment, corporal punishment was abolished entirely in England. The committee at that time said:
We have been unable to find any body of facts or figures showing that the introduction of a power of flogging has produced a decrease in the number of the offences for which it may be imposed, or that offences for which flogging may be ordered have tended to increase when little use was made of the power to order flogging or to decrease when the power was exercised more frequently. We are not satisfied that corporal punishment has that exceptionally effective influence as a deterrent which is usually claimed for it by those who advocate its use as a penalty for adult offenders.
The committee went on to say that they did not limit their investigation to the law as it then stood. They considered also the possible use of corporal punishment for other offences but came to similar conclusions. In particular, they concluded that this penalty was especially unsuitable for sexual offences, which incidentally formed the bulk of the offences in Canada for which corporal punishment was applied in those figures which I mentioned earlier.
This report is of tremendous interest and I commend it to every member of the house who concerns himself with this subject. The
Criminal Code
committee approached the widest possible variety of sources, people like the association of chief police officers of England and Wales, and the commissioner of police of the metropolis, who incidentally declined the invitation on the ground that it was not the policy of the association or in his view the function of the police to comment on the ways in which offenders are tried and dealt with by the courts.
However, a unanimous opinion was reached by that group, the police officers. It was unanimously agreed that if judicial corporal punishment were reintroduced, the police should not be required to administer it. Other sources of information were approached. The press was informed and in fact it assisted by soliciting a large number of letters commenting on the question. This public opinion poll which I mentioned earlier, the results of which were published in March, 1960, indicated that 74 per cent of the population considered that corporal punishment should be the penalty for some offences. People like the judges of the Queen's bench division and other persons concerned with the administration of criminal law were approached and the result was that a great majority of those consulted agreed that the reintroduction of judicial corporal punishment in certain circumstances might be desirable.
There was a minority of that group who differed. The members of the magistrates association of England and Wales were approached, and a vote on the question indicated that 4,412 favoured abolishing corporal punishment and 1,886 favoured its retention. The national association of probation officers was approached and submitted their findings as a group. They indicated that 89.7 per cent of their group favoured the abolition of corporal punishment. Other sources were approached, and some very interesting opinions were put forward. I shall not go through them in any detail but some of them are of passing interest. Surprisingly, the report says:
Several of our correspondents suggested that females should be liable to judicial corporal punishment as well as males. They argued that in these days women and girls were often involved in the commission of crimes of violence or other offences for which men and boys might receive this penalty, and that therefore there was no justification for treating the sexes differently.
This view, the report goes on to say, was not shared by most of the witnesses. There were points of view expressed, and certainly I have heard similar views expressed in this country, to the effect that corporal punishment should be applied as an alternative to a sentence in prison or in a corrective institution. The theory is, apparently,

Criminal Code
that this is a cheaper method and that if our corrective institutions are overcrowded it will avoid congesting them further. Little thought, I suggest, was given to whether this punishment would do any good. The report goes on to say-and I think this is an important factor in any discussion of this problem-
A striking fact that emerges from a study of the views expressed to us is that different people reach different conclusions on the basis of the same facts or experiences.
This certainly is true not only in regard to this matter but with regard to capital punishment as well. The report goes on:
It is clear also that individual views on judicial corporal punishment are greatly influenced by emotion, often arising from personal experience.
Most people's reaction in the case of certain crimes which they regard as being particularly heinous is that those responsible should be given a taste of their own medicine. The statistical evidence is examined in great detail and, again, the case for the deterrent quality of corporal punishment simply does not emerge from the facts and figures produced. One interesting comment had to do with the stability of the persons to whom corporal punishment was applied. The report says:
In general, the more stable the personality the less harm such punishment would be likely to do.
Of course, conversely, medical witnesses were agreed that if an individual already had a substantial element of resentment in his make-up, judicial corporal punishment would be likely to make it worse. Then, of course, there is the situation that the more stable the person the less harm such punishment is likely to do. The converse, of course, is true that the most unstable people, who surely represent the greater threat to society, would be affected in the opposite way. There is further argument and discussion contained in this report, all of considerable interest, relating to the question of just how the person involved would react to corporal punishment and, in particular, the so-called younger set. The report says:
We discussed this with our medical witnesses, who agreed that while this may be true of some youths, many others, far from being afraid, would accept the risk and exploit the punishment as a means of showing they were tough and could take it. Moreover, in order to maintain their status in the eyes of their associates, many who had received judicial corporal punishment would be likely to commit further offences to show that they had not been intimidated.
This is a fact which we cannot overlook in dealing with the psychology of the gang or juvenile delinquent groups in our society.
The report, of course, inquired into various areas of the commonwealth and different

countries in the world and found that in the main there was no important movement for extending corporal punishment or, in those countries which had abolished it, any important movement to have it restored. The arguments in favour of corporal punishment as a deterrent are developed and found wanting, and corporal punishment in relation to modern penological methods fails, of course, on its first application. Every movement we have made in our penal institutions and penal methods is moving away from this kind of approach. There are a number of other matters which come into the question, one of the more important of which is the problem posed by the delay between the sentencing and the carrying out of the sentence. The report concludes on this question:
We agree that the delay is the most serious practical objection to judicial corporal punishment.
The practical question arises of who is to administer this punishment whether it is by lash, or whip or strap. The policemen do not want to do it; the guards do not want to do it and, certainly, those involved in the rehabilitation aspect of prison life would not want to be associated with an activity of this kind, for after all, they are trying to develop a more positive social conscience in the individual concerned while offering some help on the road back to good citizenship. Perhaps the solution would be to hire a public whipping man, as we now have a public hangman, who would go from place to place, as travelling dentists and doctors do in our society today.
The report makes eight basic recommendations and I should like to run very quickly through them. I would remind members of the house again, that 77 per cent of the people consulted in Britain favoured the restoration or retention of criminal punishment. This committee, having examined the facts, came to the conclusion, in spite of that evidence of public opinion, that corporal punishment should not be reintroduced in Britain, and the comment is:
If that were to be done it would be putting the clock back not 12 hours but a hundred years.
Second, the present demand for the reintroduction of judicial corporal punishment seems to be limited to this country.-
Third, we consider that, in these circumstances, the reintroduction of judicial corporal punishment could be justified only if there was a reasonable assurance that it would substantially reduce crime and afford real protection to potential victims. We think that there cannot be any such assurance.
Fourth, judicial corporal punishment is out of line with modern penal methods and would militate against the success of reformative treatment, such as probation or borstal training.
The report goes on to deal in particular with some of the practical and constructive alternatives such as the physical expansion

of institutions, equipment, teaching and training, and an increase in the police forces in the various areas with a high crime incidence. This again is a constructive, logical and practical approach to the question.
Having already delayed the house too long, I would sum up by saying that it seems to be the pattern here and wherever this question has been argued and examined that public opinion in the main favours the retention of corporal punishment, but those groups that are confronted with serious study of the question and the evidence given by qualified persons in the many fields related to criminology inevitably come to the conclusion, which forms the basis of the proposition I now put to this house, that corporal punishment should be abolished in Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of this resolution. I shall make my remarks as brief as possible because I see we have only about 35 minutes left in this debate and I am sure there are many other hon. members who would like to participate. I would not wish to deny anyone who wished to make a contribution the opportunity of doing so.
I am well aware that there is a biblical injunction which says, "Spare the rod and spoil the child". I suppose there are some who would use that as a justification for the use of whipping in connection with crime. I imagine that it is possible for some to look upon the latter as an extension of the former. To me however, there seems to be no connection whatever between the two. The one was meant to be administered by a loving parent as a corrective measure for a person who had not yet achieved the age of reason or matured sufficiently to be able to reason things out for himself. The other is administered by society as a deterrent to crime. If there is any justification whatever for the use of whipping it must be as a deterrent.
The deterrent value of whipping itself is very much open to debate. Certainly it cannot be expected to have much effect upon individuals who have not yet achieved mental or psychological maturity. Even if we accept the argument that it does deter normal persons then we are arguing that the ends justify the means. I have not been able to accept that as a general rule. There may be certain exceptions to that but I have never come across any of them and in any case I feel it is not a very strong argument.
In matters of this kind I feel we should be guided by a higher principle. That principle is inherent in our concept of the nature
Criminal Code
of man himself, the principle of human dignity. Whatever deterrent value whipping may have for normal persons it does not lie so much in the pain associated with it as in the indignity to the person who has to undergo it. Human dignity is a quality each of us brings with us when we enter the world. So long as we are rational human beings it stays with us, regardless of what crimes we may commit. It would be a very sad state of affairs if the human dignity of a person depended on the varying judgments of the people around him.
This concept in my opinion goes to the very root of our society because it marks off the fundamental difference between our democracy and a society based on an atheistic materialism, the difference between a society based on the concept of the worth and dignity of the individual as a human being and a society built on the concept that man is nothing but a mere animal. Even in the case of animals, we have laws which would prohibit the use of such practices.
As a matter of principle alone-the principle of individual worth and human dignity inherent in man as a created being-I believe that this practice should be abolished. There is nothing at all sentimental about that. It is purely a matter of principle. I think we must make up our minds with respect to principles of this kind. Either we believe certain things or we do not. If we believe that a man, as an individual being, has dignity and worth within himself then the use of whipping for any reason whatever is a contradiction of that belief.
It is these contradictions that have hindered the spread of democracy in this century. People in other nations see that we profess one thing and practise another. I welcome this bill because I believe it asserts a fundamental principle of democracy and one that should govern all our legislation and practices.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
support this bill, Mr. Speaker, and I congratulate the hon. member on again having introduced it. I am not supporting it because of sentiment; I am supporting it on principle and as a result of 25 years study of corporal punishment. The reason I support this bill is that from my experience of 20 years as a member of the British Columbia legislature and my eight years in the House of Commons I have not found any evidence whatever to indicate that corporal punishment, either as a judicial sentence or as a disciplinary measure inside an institution, has acted as a deterrent to further crime or helped to rehabilitate the individual concerned to a social life and a social consciousness.

Criminal Code
I should like to ask all thoughtful members in this house-and I am certain that every one is a thoughtful member-to note that Canada is one of only two countries in the modern and civilized world where corporal punishment can be inflicted as a judicial sentence. Canada is one of only three countries in the modern civilized world where corporal punishment can be used either as a judicial sentence or as a disciplinary measure.
I ask hon. members who are here, thereby evidencing their interest in this bill-and I ask the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) to take note of this fact-to take this opportunity to wipe out one of the most archaic sentences existing in the civilized world. This matter is one which, if studied, will positively sicken you. How many hon. members in the house today have seen the board to which a man is strapped, either horizontally if he is to be paddled, or reclining if he is to be lashed? How many have seen a man with his feet fastened to the floor? How many have seen the paddle, which is a strap with holes in it, the purpose of the holes being to perforate the flesh? How many have seen the lash, the cat-o'-nine tails, with the nine strands of nylon cord? I have. I have been in the institutions and I have seen those boards. I have seen the paddle with the holes in it and I have seen the lash with blood on it. I have seen them. How many considering this matter have seen a man whose back has been lashed so that the blood is drawn and he is put in the penitentiary hospital for 10 days? I have seen these things, sir; the paddle, the lash, the board, the blood and the back.
We in Canada maintain that we are a civilized people. We maintain in this House of Commons-and we rightfully maintain-that we are spending millions upon millions of dollars to put in institutions those who commit crimes against society, for two purposes; to punish them for their crimes and to try to rehabilitate them so that they become useful members of society. What is the experience of those who have investigated this matter of whether corporal punishment deters from crime or rehabilitates prisoners as useful members of society? May I give one experience. A few years ago I went into a penitentiary in Canada and I asked the warden if he would call into his office everyone in that institution who had had the lash or the paddle. He did. I questioned every one of those men. If my memory is correct there were 12 or 13. Of those who had had the lash and the paddle, only one said that it did him any good. All the rest said it created a sense of antagonism, of violence, of hatred, of wanting to get back, not only at the individual who

had done it, not only at the warden and the magistrate who had ordered it, but at society which allowed it to be done. That was my personal experience in a penitentiary of Canada.
What I think perhaps is of more account is the report which will be found in volume II of the three year study by the joint committee of the other place and the House of Commons on capital and corporal punishment. In the appendix to volume II will be found the report of an interview carried out by our counsel in the city of Toronto with a number of men who had received the lash and the paddle, some of them many times. Some of them had been out of an institution for over 20 years, and they were asked whether the punishment deterred or not. If hon. members will read that report they will get the answer. They will find only two who said it did them any good. They will find in the report on the others words such as these- since many of these men are now well-known businessmen in Toronto initials are used. With respect to Mr. "A" we find the following:
He considered it had done him no good. He repeated several times that the strap had no effect in controlling his conduct. He did not want to give the prison authorities any satisfaction. He had gained prestige in the institution after having corporal punishment, particularly because he did not yell.
Again, we find this:
Corporal punishment was like strapping a person every once in a while to show him who was boss; it was no way to reform a man.
Hon. members can go through the report- I have it all marked-and they will see the reaction of those who were interviewed. What is the opinion arrived at? My own personal interviews with those in the institution and the interviews conducted by the counsel of the joint committee with those who had become rehabilitated, and who had received the strap, indicate to me that it did no good.
I want to add just one more statement. I wish to relate the experience I had in speaking to a man of his reaction to receiving the paddle many years ago. He thought he did not deserve it but he got it. His reaction was, "I wanted to kill the man who ordered it, and I will kill the man who gave it to me". This man told me himself that after discharge the first thing he did was to get a rifle. He went back outside the fence, and he had the guard who gave him the paddle in his sights, and he was just within seconds of becoming a murderer. The reason he did not become a murderer was that he had forgotten to take off the safety catch of the rifle and his pal grabbed the rifle away from him.
The evidence is conclusive that corporal punishment is no deterrent to further crime.

Criminal Code
[n the majority of cases it creates a reaction which is opposed to the purpose for which the House of Commons votes money, namely to try to rehabilitate as useful citizens those who have broken the laws of society. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in seconding the motion for the second reading of this bill to abolish corporal punishment. I have lever been in a penitentiary and have never seen a whip, so maybe I am talking of something about which I do not know too much.
However, in the first world war I was attached to a group from South Africa, and I know that if the negroes in the outfit had done something wrong they were hung up and lashed. I did not see them lashed but I saw them hanging there. They were tied to a cross and their backs were marked where they had been whipped. I think this is degrading.
As far as I am concerned I do not even like to see a horse whipped, let alone a human being. In fact, I am speaking the truth when I say that in Belgium after the war Canadian soldiers would go right out on to the street and pound the drivers of big wagons drawn by Canadian army horses because the drivers were whipping the horses which were hauling the loads that were too heavy. I saw that happen three or four times. As I say, I do not like to see a horse whipped, let alone a human being. It is degrading and I cannot see how any good comes from it because it only stirs up resentment. As the last speaker said, and apparently he knows what he is talking about, a man treated in this way gets murder in his heart.
We have been raised a little differently and I think we have been too long in doing away with such punishment. We should now abolish whipping. According to our teaching it is wrong and, whether we are Christian, Moslem or whatever we are, let us get rid of it by voting for abolition today.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I took part in a debate on a similar bill in 1959 at which time I spoke in favour of abolition of such punishment. I do not propose to review, except briefly, some of the points I made at that time because I still maintain the same views. To those who may turn to the debates of that year, may I say that I quoted from the study of the British committee into the deterrent aspects of the use of flogging and the lash. It seemed to me and to those who made that study, I believe, that there was no deterrent effect whatsoever; that a person was just as apt to be a recidivist without the lash as if he were the type to whom such punishment was administered. The figures and findings of that study may be found in the debate of two years ago.
One point I should like to make this afternoon is that whether or not we pass this measure, and I think there are others who have views they would like to express, the fact remains that the use of corporal punishment is regarded as outmoded in Canada, and that can be proved by the statistics relating to those who have undergone such punishment. In 1959 the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) pointed out that in 1931 about 12.1 per cent of those who

Criminal Code
were eligible to receive such punishment did in fact receive it and that by 1954 this figure had gone down to .6 per cent. If I may make a comparison in a different way, out of 500 prisoners who would have been eligible to receive corporal punishment in 1931 some 60 or 61 did receive it in that year, whereas in 1954 only three out of a similar group of 500 eligible to receive such punishment did in fact receive it. So the shrinkage is most apparent.
I also have great faith in the approach of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) to the whole problem of punishment and rehabilitation of the criminal. If the measure of the hon. member for York-Scarborough is not passed this afternoon, I am sure we can hopefully anticipate that something will be done in the not too distant future, perhaps next session if not later this session. This is only a personal hope but I know that the Minister of Justice, with his vast depth of humanity and his great interest in the proper carrying out of his duties, will take us off the hook, for we as civilized people must surely feel rather ashamed and guilty that we are among the very small handful of nations still using such methods.

speechtext: One of three.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
One of three, says the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who very kindly identified the other two in response to a question of mine a few minutes ago.
There is yet another point I should like to make and as it has been made before I will not press it ad nauseam. The use of the lash or flogging is apt to put a special brand, almost like the mark of Cain, upon the person who undergoes such treatment and, as previous speakers have indicated, it is apt to turn the punished person into a criminal seeking revenge. We heard the very graphic story of the hon. member for Vancouver East about the man whose first thought upon leaving the penitentiary was to purchase a rifle-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Reform school; he was only 17 years old.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH IMPOSITION OF CORPORAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
-and to seek revenge. It was reform school. I thank the hon. member for putting me straight. A very important aspect to remember is that we can turn a criminal who might be helped into a savage animal. The support, if any support there is, that society gives to the use of the lash I think would be in regard to very special types of cases; not only the case involving violence on another person, but more likely the case involving a criminal who has sexually molested a little child. Here, when

speaking to members of the public one does find, especially if one is a parent or talks to a parent, the greatest abhorrence of this type of person and a feeling almost perhaps without reason, so terrified are parents of this type of person in society. I believe that in this area you would find the chief support for the use of the lash. My answer to that support is that such criminals obviously are very sick indeed and have to be cured by other methods. I do not think it would deter them for one single instant to undergo this savage and mediaeval punishment.
Finally, sir, I am not going to discuss the esoteric subject of the effect of spanking upon Toronto businessmen, but the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) quoted the Biblical injunction, spare the rod and spoil the child. I think that the rod does have its place in society; there has to be a certain chastisement offered, but that is a prerogative of the home where the very young may have certain impressions made upon them by the parents who believe in the use of the rod. I think, however, when one reaches an adult stage habits are formed, and it is too late to start meting out physical punishment upon malefactors.
For these reasons, sir, and mainly because I do not think that the lash has any practical value whatsoever, I certainly support the bill of the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee).

Mr. Speaker, this very important subject is being brought forward again by the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), and there has been considerable debate on it in the past. I feel most of the speakers have been in favour of the bill, which is against corporal punishment. They have spoken in favour of abolition I think in the same manner as those who are against capital punishment. They seem to be emotional, as are those who speak against forms of capital punishment, but they are more vociferous. Perhaps there are admittedly more today who are against corporal punishment than there are against capital punishment. Nevertheless, there are still many who do not make their thoughts known in this chamber or outside and who still feel that we should in some way retain these two forms of punishment.
I do not have definite views myself, but I do feel that some of the expressions in favour of retention have not been put forward, except by the member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith) in the debate last year. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who is a very interested student of

penology and has been for some years, has delivered his informed but emotional speech. I take exception to the example he used of the successful businessmen. They were asked in the questionnaire that was sent out by the 1954 committee whether in their opinion corporal punishment had been of any value in their own careers. I suggest very seriously, Mr. Speaker, that these now respectable citizens would not admit or appreciate the fact, just as members of this house might not admit openly that school punishment had played a very important part in their careers. So the figures in those instances again do not give the whole story. It would be interesting to have figures, and I have not seen any, in respect of those who have not been successful; those who still follow a life of crime, to ascertain whether they had received punishment or not, to what degree, and the part it played in their careers.
